title: Cardinals QB Gardner Minshew update
summary: The Arizona Cardinals have started three quarterbacks this season. After starter Jacoby Brissett was shipped off to Baltimore, the job was handed to Gardner Minshew. He lasted one full game. Minshew landed on IR and on Monday, he had surgery.   RELATED: CARDINALS SIGN VETERAN QUARTERBACK In the first half of the divisional battle with […]
full_text: SEATTLE, WASHINGTON - NOVEMBER 08: Dante Fowler Jr. #56 of the Seattle Seahawks knocks the ball out of the hands of Gardner Minshew II #15 of the Arizona Cardinals during the second quarter at Lumen Field on November 08, 2026 in Seattle, Washington. (Photo by Steph Chambers/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Arizona Cardinals have started three quarterbacks this season. After starter Jacoby Brissett was shipped off to Baltimore, the job was handed to Gardner Minshew. He lasted one full game. Minshew landed on IR and on Monday, he had surgery. RELATED: CARDINALS SIGN VETERAN QUARTERBACK In the first half of the divisional battle with the Seattle Seahawks in Week 9, Minshew suffered an injury, but finished out the contest. The severity of his injury did not become known until later. Cardinals QB Gardner Minshew on Monday underwent surgery to repair his torn UCL, per me and @joshweinfuss . He’s doing well and should make a full recovery for the 2027 season. — Jeremy Fowler (@JFowlerESPN) November 18, 2026 It is not known if Gardner Minshew will return off of IR this year. He underwent season-ending surgery on Monday, November 16, 2026, to repair a torn ulnar collateral ligament (UCL) in his right elbow, which just happens to be his throwing arm. Most likely, he won’t be playing again this season. He is expected to make a full recovery and will return to the field at some point. This type injury is usually one that baseball pitchers suffer, but tends not to be as severe for the throwing motion of a quarterback. But make no mistake, an UCL injury is serious. In the NFL, the most recent UCL injury was when San Francisco 49ers quarterback Brock Purdy damaged his UCL in 2023 and had surgery. He played the entire season the following year and won a Super Bowl. Currently in the Cardinals QB room is rookie Carson Beck, journeyman Josh Johnson, and rookie Joey Aguaiar. Minshew is currently on a one-year contract he inked this past spring and is scheduled to be a free agent after the season unless he is extended.

title: Cardinals hand Chiefs an infrequent gift
summary: The Kansas City Chiefs host the Arizona Cardinals this weekend. The Chiefs are one of the best clubs in the AFC and one of four teams with identical 7-2-0 records. Which means they are a really good team.   With this game, Arizona is giving the Chiefs a rare occurrence on any team’s regular season […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CA - SEPTEMBER 13: Isaac Seumalo #73 of the Arizona Cardinals drops back to block during an NFL football game against the Los Angeles Chargers at SoFi Stadium on September 13, 2026 in Inglewood, California. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Kansas City Chiefs host the Arizona Cardinals this weekend. The Chiefs are one of the best clubs in the AFC and one of four teams with identical 7-2-0 records. Which means they are a really good team. With this game, Arizona is giving the Chiefs a rare occurrence on any team’s regular season schedule. RELATED: JORDAN BURCH LOST FOR SEASON The Cardinals are showing they are a hot mess and one of the worst teams in the league, currently at 3-7-0. Kansas City has the opportunity to play in this year’s AFC Championship Game the way they are playing. Five of their nine contests, the Chiefs have scored 30+ points. But there are obstacles on their schedule. That begins the week after playing Arizona. The Chiefs are on the road on Thanksgiving Day against the Buffalo Bills. Currently, the Bills are the AFC’s best team with an 8-1-0 record. They have a 3-1 home record and are the league’s highest-scoring team with 287 points. Needless to say, this is an important game for both the Bills and Chiefs. As the season begins to dwindle, both clubs are assured of making the playoff whether as a division winner or a lower seed. However, with these two clubs, the Number 1 seed in this year’s postseason just might be at stake. Here’s the rub: The Chiefs against the Bills on Thursday in a huge matchup is just four days after playing the Cardinals. Usually, this is a major issue. There isn’t time to have a player’s day off or have any meaningful practice sessions in order to get ready for the next opponent and gameplan. Not to mention the colossal matchup pitting Buffalo against Kansas City. The loser suddenly starts to backpedal and, in all likelihood, gets sent to the bottom of the playoff contenders, whereas the winner is king of the mountain. By playing the Cardinals first, the Chiefs have the opportunity to rest some starters in order to save them for the Bills, which also guarantees they won’t become injured. This is usually the norm in the final game of the season for certain clubs that are already in the playoffs and have nothing to gain with a win. Teams have been known to start their entire second team offensive and defensive units in contests such as this. But never during the meat of the schedule. It is very possible that Kansas City could run their starters in the first quarter, or even the first half, and then insert the second teamers for the remainder of the game. Arizona has been outscored 51-9 in their past two games. Their offense cannot run the ball, and are starting the third quarterback this year behind an offensive line full of Band-Aids and backups to backups. The team has scored less than 24 points in a game seven out of nine contests. Three games, less than 10 points. They have the seventh fewest scoring offense. The defense is tied for allowing the most points (289). Kansas City is 4–0 at Arrowhead Stadium this season and holds an average margin of victory of 15.8 points at home, the second-best mark in the NFL. However, it is not exactly about one team looking beyond this week’s opponent and thinking they are going to breeze by without trying. Playing their second teamers against what Arizona is putting on the field just might become a fair fight. Look at the Cardinals’ current starting lineup on offense compared to Week 1: QB3 RB2, RB3, RB PS WR4, WR5, WR6 TE1, TE2, TE IR RT1 RG1 C2 LG1 LT3 The entire Cardinals roster is a hot mess. Which is “Advantage Kansas City.”

title: Bye Week Roundtable: The Falcons are stuck in the mud
summary: Entering the bye week on a losing streak was likely for the Falcons, given their recent opponents. Facing the Bengals and Chiefs in consecutive weeks will leave most teams scrambling for answers. What is alarming in Atlanta is how lifeless and helpless the recent performances have been, including in a matchup against a far lesser […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GEORGIA - NOVEMBER 15: Kendal Daniels #53 of the Atlanta Falcons tackles Emmett Johnson #10 of the Kansas City Chiefs during the fourth quarter at Mercedes-Benz Stadium on November 15, 2026 in Atlanta, Georgia. (Photo by Todd Kirkland/Getty Images) | Getty Images Entering the bye week on a losing streak was likely for the Falcons, given their recent opponents. Facing the Bengals and Chiefs in consecutive weeks will leave most teams scrambling for answers. What is alarming in Atlanta is how lifeless and helpless the recent performances have been, including in a matchup against a far lesser team than Kansas City or Cincinnati put on the field. From being manhandled in the trenches against Tampa Bay to having no answers against Cincinnati in Madrid to never posing a threat against the Chiefs, it’s hard to find positives about the Falcons right now. The bye week couldn’t be coming at a better time for Kevin Stefanski. It’s also an ideal time to put together a roundtable with Tre’Shon Diaz and Kevin Knight. We’ll dive into some of the most pressing topics surrounding the franchise’s current state. What has gone wrong for Tommy Rees after an encouraging start? Allen Strk: Where to begin? The lack of play-action efficiency is glaring, but the frequent stubbornness in calling predictable screens and ineffective jumbo packages has been just as jarring. The coaching staff isn’t learning much from previous game tape. Opposing defenses are consistently breaking on screens before the ball is even released. Several of these failures occur on third downs, which completely neutralizes them. In short-yardage scenarios, they attempt to use extra tight ends and offensive linemen to generate extra push. That has rarely worked, yet those packages continue to be consistently used. They struggle to function playing from behind and operate with a total lack of confidence on third-and-longs. They also aren’t recognizing where the unit is falling short, and they fail to effectively utilize their premium talent. Bijan Robinson’s extraordinary skill set hasn’t come close to being maximized. He is rarely featured as a pass-catcher outside of a swing pass or checkdown. For all the effort put into Michael Penix Jr.’s development, the coaching staff has lost sight of featuring the team’s best players not named Drake London. That includes Kyle Pitts, who is largely an afterthought until the team is down by three possessions in the second half. Tre’Shon Diaz: Rees’ offense lacks balance, discipline, and rhythm. The offensive line was already declining as an outside zone unit. They’ve struggled to adjust to the newly implemented gap-scheme concepts. They also can’t stop committing penalties. Jawaan Taylor’s false start troubles are no surprise, but that sickness is spreading. Holding penalties have cost the team lately. It’s hard to get into a rhythm when you’re shooting yourself in the foot. It doesn’t help that Michael Penix is missing open receivers throughout the game. Rees has struggled to establish game flow, as his attempts to get Penix comfortable aren’t working. Kevin Knight: I think the simplest explanation is that Rees/Stefanski came in prepared to run a certain offense, and the Falcons do not have the personnel to execute it. We’ve talked about the transition to more diverse run schemes and more emphasis on the screen game as an answer to pressure. The offensive line is sort of trapped between schemes, the screen game is sloppy, and Michael Penix is not able to hit the short throws with consistency. It’s sort of a toxic stew that is really exposing Rees/Stefanski’s inability to adapt the scheme to their talent. Should the Falcons be concerned about A.J. Terrell long-term? Allen Strk: There has to be genuine concern when all the positive attributes are non-existent. Terrell isn’t physical at the line of scrimmage, disrupting the receiver’s timing and rhythm. His route recognition hasn’t been there to jump on targets in his direction. His tackling has been disastrous, as he missed four against Tampa Bay. Worst of all, the simplest double moves are baiting him out of position. It’s one thing for Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins to have their way with you. For Cyrus Allen to win on a stop-and-go to torch you for a highlight-reel touchdown is troubling. Quarterbacks aren’t hesitant to target Terrell. It happened on opening day against the Steelers, when Aaron Rodgers found Roman Wilson and D.K. Metcalf open downfield after beating Terrell at the line of scrimmage. The veteran corner was forced to interfere before the ball arrived, albeit somehow the one on Metcalf wasn’t penalized. If things don’t improve, the front office will have to assess his future, because you don’t want a liability on the roster who is being paid like a top-tier player. Tre’Shon Diaz: I do think there’s cause for concern if the team expects him to regain All-Pro status. Corners rarely sustain their peaks for more than five years. That’s how long it’s been since the corner was named an All-Pro. Terrell is losing reps to everyone right now, not just Chase. It’s fair to suspect that his groin injury is still hampering him, but that’s another reason his longevity could be called into question. He’s missed six games in the last two seasons and will be 30 at the start of 2028. The hope is that he can recover and be viable in 2027 before the regime has to make a tough call. Kevin Knight: You kind of have to be after his play this season. I still think a fair amount of it is health-related, but even so, Terrell is making way too much money to be such a liability. He’ll have the rest of the season to get healthier and prove that this first half was an aberration. If he doesn’t, there aren’t really many good options for the Falcons. They still owe Terrell a ton of money in 2027. There isn’t an easy way out of the contract. Most likely, he’ll be with the team through next season regardless of his play this year. Does the offensive line need two tackles next season, or can Jake Matthews be counted on as a starter for one more year? Allen Strk: As much as the Falcons need to revamp their offensive line, replacing two tackles in the same off-season is extremely difficult. The troubling state of offensive line play across the league has been a talking point for years. Look no further than the potential market. With the best potential available tackle options being Warren McClendon Jr. and Ikem Ekwonu, with the latter coming off a severe injury, the front office will likely be forced to go in another direction. They should absolutely draft a later-round prospect to develop under and compete with Matthews, who is an ineffective run blocker and becoming more penalty-prone. The group desperately needs more of an anchor on outside runs. Jawaan Taylor is too sluggish getting out of his stance and gives far too many easy tells, as J.J. Watt brilliantly broke down. Despite needing a new right tackle and Matthews being serviceable at best, they won’t have the bandwidth to add two surefire starters next year. Tre’Shon Diaz: You can argue that the Falcons should do what they can to upgrade both, but that’s easier said than done. Franchise tackles rarely hit the market. The team would need to invest a high draft pick to acquire one. Pulling off both moves in the same offseason while also trying to upgrade the center position may prove too difficult. Matthews has been reliable as a pass protector after a slow start and an early-season injury. The run game would suffer on the left side for one more year, but if the team fills the other holes on the line, they should be able to compensate. Kevin Knight: I think Jake Matthews can hold it down for one more season. He’ll also probably have to. It does help contract-wise. The Falcons can come up with one tackle via free agency or (more likely) a high pick in the 2027 NFL Draft. Adding two new tackles is almost impossible. Best-case scenario would be a top tackle addition and…

title: 3 up and 3 down: The Midseason Edition
summary: The Atlanta Falcons have played roughly 60% of their games, so this is the perfect time for a midseason 3 up and 3 down to see whose stock has risen the most and who’s taken the biggest hit. Here’s the Week 10 edition. 3 up Drake London The touchdown numbers have taken a hit, but […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GA - NOVEMBER 15: Drake London (5) of the Atlanta Falcons breaks free of the Kansas City Chiefs defense during the Sunday afternoon NFL game between the Atlanta Falcons and the Kansas City Chiefs on November 15, 2026 at the Mercedes-benz Stadium in Atlanta, GA. (Photo by David J. Griffin/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Atlanta Falcons have played roughly 60% of their games, so this is the perfect time for a midseason 3 up and 3 down to see whose stock has risen the most and who’s taken the biggest hit. Here’s the Week 10 edition. 3 up Drake London The touchdown numbers have taken a hit, but don’t get it twisted, Drake London has been worth every penny. I know he had a drop in the Chiefs game, but that’s a rare occurrence for the wideout; it was only his second this season. This man has dealt with constant quarterback shuffling, bad offensive coordinators, and no consistent running mate, but he still gets the job done. Heading into the bye, London has the 7th-most receiving yards in the league, and his inaccurate quarterback is suppressing those numbers. He’s the best blocking receiver on the team, and you never have to worry about his effort. You’re always going to get the best version of him. Drake London adds to his HUGE night @ATLvsGB on Prime Video Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/0nWsw3vuwJ — NFL (@NFL) September 25, 2026 Gervon Dexter Sr. Dexter was one of a handful of players who got an in-season extension , and he’s been living up to it. He’s second in pressures (30) on the team, the 5th most among all interior defensive linemen, and his 15.2 pass-rush win rate is 6th best for his position. He also has the second most sacks on the team. Acquired via trade right before the season, he had a lot to prove in this new environment but has fit well in this attacking front. He still needs work in the run game; he doesn’t handle doubles well, but he still has the 3rd most run stops on the team with 10. If he can keep improving that area of his game, he’ll be one of the best overall interior players in the league. Chris Lindstrom There may be issues on this offensive line, but Lindstrom is not one of them. In true pass sets, he’s only allowed eight pressures and one sack across 10 games. He’s also shown that he can play in this new scheme and be a weapon as a puller. Unfortunately, he’s playing next to arguably the worst run-blocking tackle in the league, and his former center, Ryan Neuzil, wasn’t a fit, making it even harder for Lindstrom to thrive. Doesn’t matter to Lindstrom; he’s shown up every week and done his job. The team needs to get him some help this offseason so he’s not doing it alone. Chris Lindstrom had one of the best performances of his career last night. He's doing it all in this revitalized run scheme. Elite at climbing to the 2nd level. Finally getting opportunities as a puller. Had multiple 2 for 1s & consistently moved the Saints DL off their spots pic.twitter.com/SNxddB0MIG — Tre’Shon (@tre3shon) October 6, 2026 Honorable Mentions: Sydney Brown, Bijan Robinson, and LaCale London 3 down Michael Penix Jr It’s been a mixed bag for the quarterback, and that’s not what you want to hear when you’re auditioning for your future. At this rate, I am not confident he’ll get his 5th-year option picked up. There have been flashes of good quarterback play, but not enough to give anyone confidence he’s the franchise’s future. The Falcons need the quarterback that showed up to the 49ers game, not the one they’ve had since. While accuracy has always been an issue, Penix has done a good job of protecting the ball, but we aren’t seeing that this year. Lately, his good play doesn’t come until the game is out of hand. It also isn’t a good sign that in the 2/3 wins where he looked good, his backfield put up 200 yards on the ground. He isn’t elevating the offense, and he is cracking under pressure while facing it at the second-lowest rate (28.7%) in the league . Penix isn’t playing for his 5th year anymore; he’s playing for his job in 2027. If the team keeps losing, they may end up with the opportunity to grab a new quarterback or feel forced to spend more money than they’d like on the market. Off target, missing open guys, and putting the ball in harms way. It's hard to win football games and build any sort of momentum playing like this. pic.twitter.com/c7yiogOxmE — Tre’Shon (@tre3shon) November 16, 2026 Divine Deablo A player many of us had hoped would become a piece for the future is playing himself out of Atlanta. Deablo has been bad out of the gate. His play recognition has regressed, and he looks like a shell of himself. He was dealing with a hamstring to start the season and is once again wearing a club. The team scratched him for the Chiefs game, and hopefully the bye week does his body some good. Unfortunately, injuries are a feature of his player profile. He’s missed time every year of his career with something, and you can’t commit significant dollars to someone who can’t stay on the field. AJ Terrell When cornerbacks fall off, they fall hard. This season had the makings of a special storyline with the addition of his younger brother ; now the Falcons have to handle this situation carefully to prevent any bad blood. There were some lapses before Terrell went on IR, but since coming back, he’s been a disaster. It’s one thing to get torched by Ja’Marr Chase; it’s another to get worked by Cyrus Allen, giving him his first touchdown of the year. There is no easy out of this contract; the best the Falcons can hope for is that he comes off the bye, looks serviceable, and gives them enough confidence to roll into 2027 for one last ride. Filthy route from Cyrus Allen 😮‍💨 pic.twitter.com/YNh2IdJZjU — NFL (@NFL) November 15, 2026 Dishonorable Mentions: Mike Hughes, Jawaan Taylor, and Olamide Zaccheaus The Falcons have seven games left, and everyone on this list has a chance to improve or lower their stock heading into the offseason. It ain’t over till it’s over, and this evaluation period will be critical in helping the Falcons build their 2027 roster. Who will you be keeping an eye on during the final stretch?

title: Ravens activate RB Adam Randall from injured reserve
summary: The Baltimore Ravens activated running back Adam Randall from injured reserve on Wednesday, possibly positioning the sixth-round pick to make his NFL debut on Sunday against the Panthers. The Ravens now have four IR activations remaining with two more available if they miraculously make the playoff. One is reserved for quarterback Lamar Jackson, and another […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MARYLAND - AUGUST 15: Adam Randall #23 of the Baltimore Ravens runs the ball during an NFL preseason football game against the Philadelphia Eagles at M&T Bank Stadium on August 15, 2026 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Perry Knotts/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Baltimore Ravens activated running back Adam Randall from injured reserve on Wednesday, possibly positioning the sixth-round pick to make his NFL debut on Sunday against the Panthers. The Ravens now have four IR activations remaining with two more available if they miraculously make the playoff. One is reserved for quarterback Lamar Jackson, and another could be bookmarked for kicker Tyler Loop. When center Jovaughn Gwyn went down in Week 3 with knee injury, there was some hope that he could come back at some point but no updates since. The same is true of second-year cornerback Bilhol Kone, who was designated for return when he was placed on IR during roster cuts but has yet to return to practice. Baltimore also needs to consider the possibility of key players going down in the next few weeks, which could require IR stints before late-season returns. Randall, 22, landed on injured reserve at the end of the preseason with a foot injury. What was initially suspected to be an IR stash for a young player turned out to be a more serious issue that sidelined him until Week 8. Randall returned to practice on October 28 as a full participant, but the Ravens used his full three-week practice window to preserve roster flexibility as they navigated injuries and the trade deadline. Baltimore’s run game has been stagnant for weeks, so Randall could prove some juice as a change-of-pace back. However, he is unlikely to do much better than Derrick Henry behind a struggling offensive line. Randall’s ability to contribute in the pass catching game is unlikely to be utilized given the presence of Justice Hill. However, he is no guarantee to be part of the game day picture with Rasheen Ali entrenched on special teams. As the Ravens’ season slips further and further away, they should consider giving Randall more time. His age, size, and athleticism offer an appealing developmental trajectory that could elevate him to at least a No. 2 role in the backfield while on his rookie contract. The Ravens also re-signed guard Michael Jordan to the practice squad as additional offensive line depth. He fills the spot opened by kicker Harrison Mevis’ release on Tuesday. Riley Patterson hit all four of his kicks – two short field goals and two extra points – in his team debut on Monday night, likely securing him the kicking job until Tyler Loop comes off IR.
author: Nikhil Mehta

title: Ravens discussion: Marlon Humphrey can’t leave Baltimore soon enough
summary: The Baltimore Ravens are having a miserable season. Lamar Jackson is injured. The team is losing. Fans are not happy. So when a longtime Raven, a supposed leader, a former first-round pick on a $100 million contract says that the city in which he plays is best at making “criminals,” it hits a little too […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MD - NOVEMBER 05: Marlon Humphrey #44 of the Baltimore Ravens looks on before the game against the Jacksonville Jaguars at M&T Bank Stadium on November 5, 2026 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Scott Taetsch/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Baltimore Ravens are having a miserable season. Lamar Jackson is injured. The team is losing. Fans are not happy. So when a longtime Raven, a supposed leader, a former first-round pick on a $100 million contract says that the city in which he plays is best at making “criminals,” it hits a little too close to home. Humphrey is in the final year of that deal, and between struggling on the field and antagonizing fans, he seems exceedingly unlikely to stay in Baltimore. Is it time for Humphrey’s Ravens tenure to end? Has he ruined his legacy in Baltimore and sank any chance of a potential Ring of Honor induction? Should the team even consider parting ways with him right away to send a message and start moving towards the future? Check out our takes below, and give yours in the comments section! Nikhil’s take: Humphrey has been rightfully blasted by Baltimore mayor Brandon Scott as well as plenty of former Ravens for his comments. They represented a complete disconnect with reality. Not only was Humphrey demonstrably wrong – the city’s crime issues have gotten significantly better in recent years – he also thought it was appropriate to say such a thing publicly! There’s an argument that we should all move on from this story, and we probably should – after this. But I think it’s worth noting how this fits with the current narrative about the team’s mentality. Players can have podcasts on their spare time – I personally find Humphrey’s deeply unentertaining – but turning them into a lightning rod for controversy is a selfish, anti-team attitude. He should not be causing distractions; he should be helping the team focus after five straight losses. He may have improved in recent games, but he has still allowed the most yards in coverage of any defender in the last two seasons. ‘ Parting ways with Humphrey now does not really make sense unless the team wants to send a loud-and-clear message about their desire for real change. His salary became fully guaranteed in Week 1, so there are no savings to be had unless another team makes an exceedingly unlikely waiver claims. (Vested veterans are subject to waivers after the trade deadline.) But as soon as the offseason starts, his locker should be scrubbed clean. Dustin’s take: It is a true shame to see a once fan favorite player burn any shred of good will he had remaining with the fans. Marlon Humphrey is one of the best cornerbacks in Ravens franchise history and could have been remembered fondly by fans after his playing days were over. Instead, Humphrey has decided trolling his own fans is more important than leaving behind a respectful legacy. I won’t excuse the behavior of fans who personally attack athletes on social media after poor performances, but Humphrey’s recent comments regarding the city of Baltimore extends to more than just those who may take things too far online. It is clear that Humphrey no longer wants to be a member of the Baltimore Ravens, and the feeling is mutual. The once young and hungry cornerback who left everything on the field every week has become someone that most fans can’t wait to see go. Whether this is who Humphrey has always secretly been, or if he has truly changed is a mystery to me. Now, it’s your turn! Download the app to connect with fellow diehards and share your take. Download the SB Nation app on iOS or Android .

title: Ravens DT Nnamdi Madubuike misses first practice of Week 11
summary: The Baltimore Ravens only listed six players on their first injury report of Week 11 – a marked improvement over the last month – but Nnamdi Madubuike could be at risk of missing the team’s next game against the Carolina Panthers. After Monday night’s loss to the previously-winless Chargers – yes, that phrasing is sticking around – […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - NOVEMBER 1: Nnamdi Madubuike #92 of the Baltimore Ravens reacts against the Buffalo Bills during an NFL football game at Highmark Stadium on November 1, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Baltimore Ravens only listed six players on their first injury report of Week 11 – a marked improvement over the last month – but Nnamdi Madubuike could be at risk of missing the team’s next game against the Carolina Panthers. After Monday night’s loss to the previously-winless Chargers – yes, that phrasing is sticking around – the Ravens have one less day to prepare for their trip to Carolina. Baltimore’s week-to-week injury situation has improved, but that cannot make up for the absence of star quarterback Lamar Jackson (and backup Tyler Huntley). Jacoby Brissett, who was acquired from the Cardinals before the trade deadline, performed admirably in his first game in Baltimore, but he cannot carry the Ravens’ porous defense to victory. That unit could struggle even more without Madubuike. The seventh-year defensive tackle has just one sack and zero tackles for loss in his eight games since coming back from last year’s season-ending neck injury, but he ranks second on the team with 26 pressures, per Pro Football Focus . Madubuike might be struggling to finish plays – so is Trey Hendrickson, for that matter – but he is still a disruptive force in the trenches who is better than the next man up. That could be 2025 sixth-round pick Aeneas Peebles, an undersized lineman with burst and agility in the pass rush. He was active for the Ravens’ first four games with Madubuike still ramping up but has been a health scratch since his star teammate’s return. Giving Peebles some much-deserved developmental snaps could be a small silver lining if Madubuike is absent. The Ravens listed five other players on their Wednesday injury report, which was an estimation since the team held a walkthrough. Here is the full list: Full participation OLB Mike Green (biceps) TE Matthew Hibner (hand) RB Adam Randall (neck/hamstring) Limited participation S Jaylinn Hawkins (knee) RG Vega Ioane (knee/shoulder) Did not participate DT Nnamdi Madubuike (hamstring) The Panthers are coming into Week 11 with far more injuries, though they have also seen improvements over the last few weeks. Here is Carolina’s Wednesday injury report: Full participation RB Jonathan Brooks (groin) OL Brady Christensen (hamstring) TE Feleipe Franks (wrist) LB Jackson Kuwatch (shoulder) CB Mike Jackson (groin) CB Will Lee III (hamstring) QB Bryce Young (foot) Limited participation OLB Trevis Gipson Sr. (ankle) Did not participate RB Chuba Hubbard (non-injury related/rest) LB Bobby Okereke (foot) S Isaiah Simmons (knee) TE Tommy Tremble (knee) TE Darren Waller (knee)

title: Winners and losers from the Ravens’ Week 10 loss to the Chargers
summary: The Ravens suffered their fifth straight loss in Week 10, giving the Chargers their first win of the season. There were a few bright spots in Baltimore’s loss, including the debut of a new quarterback, but plenty of blame to be handed out as well. Winners Jacoby Brissett: The Ravens’ newest quarterback was thrown straight […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MARYLAND - NOVEMBER 16: Mark Andrews #89 of the Baltimore Ravens reacts against the Los Angeles Chargers during an NFL football game at M&T Bank Stadium on November 16, 2026 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Ravens suffered their fifth straight loss in Week 10, giving the Chargers their first win of the season. There were a few bright spots in Baltimore’s loss, including the debut of a new quarterback, but plenty of blame to be handed out as well. Winners Jacoby Brissett: The Ravens’ newest quarterback was thrown straight into the fire, dropping back 51 times in his debut. While it was not a perfect performance, Brissett proved that he can operate Baltimore’s offense at a high enough level to remain competitive. The veteran journeyman flashed a connection with multiple Ravens pass catchers after being with the team only 10 days. Staying alive for a potential Lamar Jackson return down the road seems like wishful thinking after losing to an 0-8 team and falling to 4-6, but Brissett at least elevates Baltimore’s offense to a watchable status for the fans who will continue to show up. Mark Andrews: It was reported during the game that Andrews had broken his hand earlier in the season, which could explain some of the veteran tight end’s struggles this year. Andrews looked more like his old self against Los Angeles, leading the team with eight catches for 82 yards and an 87.4 grade from Pro Football Focus — all season-highs, too. Brissett seemed to have immediate chemistry with Andrews, so his production could continue to improve for the remainder of the season. Mike Green: Green was the standout on the Ravens’ defense with perhaps the best game of his career. The second-year edge rusher had the team’s only two sacks against Justin Herbert while also making several plays in the run game. Green now leads the team in sacks for the season with 5.5. Marlon Humphrey: On a defense full of highly-paid underperforming players this season, Humphrey has taken perhaps the most criticism of all. The former All-Pro showed up against the Chargers, however, leading the defense with an 82.4 PFF grade. Although it was recovered by Los Angeles, Humphrey forced a fumble on the Chargers’ first drive of the game by stripping running back Omarion Hampton. Josh Cuevas : The rookie tight end caught three passes for 37 yards, all coming during a two-minute drill drive to get a field goal before halftime. Losers Offensive line: Baltimore’s offensive line has been under fire this season, and for good reason. The unit was unable to generate anything on the ground against Los Angeles as the offense finished with an abysmal 16 yards on 15 total carries. Derrick Henry was hit in the backfield on what felt like every handoff, while the best run of the night, a 14-yard gain by Justice Hill, was nullified due to a holding penalty. Ja’Kobi Lane: Of his team-high 11 targets, Lane came down with only three catches for 61 yards. The third-round rookie was the intended target on Brissett’s interception, though the pass was slightly behind him. Lane’s biggest blunder of the night was dropping a potential touchdown just before halftime. The Ravens had to settle for a field goal instead in a game that ultimately came down to three points. Zay Flowers: The fourth-year wideout put the nail in the coffin for Baltimore with a costly fumble at the end of the game. Down by three with over two minutes left in the game, the Ravens’ offense was driving before Flowers was stripped after a 15-yard catch. His five lost fumbles since entering the league are tied for the most among wide receivers during that time. Derrick Henry: It is hard to fault Henry too much for his struggles this season with how often he has been hit in the backfield on run plays, but the future Hall of Famer still deserves some blame. Even when getting past the line of scrimmage without being hit, Henry has not shown the same ability to break tackles or make defenders miss this season. While he did reach the end zone twice against the Chargers, Henry finished the night with just 20 yards on 10 rushing attempts and only 10 yards on five receptions. Jesse Minter: Rookie head coaches deserve a grace period, especially when their team loses its MVP quarterback, but the heat may be turning up on Minter after 10 weeks. Baltimore’s defense was supposed to rebound with Minter at the helm, but the unit has been just as bad, if not worse than last season, with an improved group of players. A lack of discipline has been a major issue for the team overall, with penalties still being a weekly talking point. The players perhaps deserve the brunt of the blame, but the head coach is ultimately the one responsible for the product fielded every week.
author: Dustin Cox

title: Ravens discussion: what changes should Jesse Minter make going forward?
summary: The Baltimore Ravens are headed in the wrong direction. General manager Eric DeCosta will be responsible for the roster reset that should come this offseason, but it’s up to head coach Jesse Minter to stop the skid down the stretch. Today, let’s discuss what changes Minter needs to make for the rest of the season. […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MD - NOVEMBER 05: Head coach Jesse Minter of the Baltimore Ravens looks on during the second half against the Jacksonville Jaguars at M&T Bank Stadium on November 5, 2026 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Scott Taetsch/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Baltimore Ravens are headed in the wrong direction. General manager Eric DeCosta will be responsible for the roster reset that should come this offseason, but it’s up to head coach Jesse Minter to stop the skid down the stretch. Today, let’s discuss what changes Minter needs to make for the rest of the season. Your answer may depend on your outlook. Optimists will look for ways to keep winning games, pessimists will call for immediate overhauls. Here are my thoughts; be sure to add yours in the comments section below! Nikhil’s take: The company line out of The Castle will remain the same: keep playoff hopes alive and hope Lamar Jackson can save the season. That seems exceedingly unlikely at this point. And here’s the thing: wholesale changes looking towards the future aren’t necessarily mutually exclusive with being more competitive. If, for example, the Ravens still think Carson Vinson can be their future left tackle, he could rotate in with Ronnie Stanley, who has struggled in his own right. Elimination from playoff contention should give Vinson the starting job for the rest of the year. The front office also needs to have an uncomfortable conversation about Roquan Smith’s future in Baltimore. There’s a growing argument that Trenton Simpson could be the Ravens’ future at inside linebacker on a more mid-level contract – or a bigger move back to the 80/20 approach of years past. That would indicate Buchanan paired with a veteran – perhaps Smith for one more year or a cheap offseason acquisition – could be the long-term plan. Cornerback Marlon Humphrey and tight end Mark Andrews both had bounce-back games vs. the Chargers, so calls for their benching will likely cease. Still, the Ravens should continue to work in T.J. Tampa and rookies Matt Hibner and Josh Cuevas. Getting third-round rookie Ja’Kobi Lane more opportunities – even after a tough showing on Monday night – is a must, and seeing what Devontez Walker and Elijah Sarratt can do isn’t a bad idea, either. Now, it’s your turn! What should Minter change for the rest of the season? Let us know in the comments section below!
author: Nikhil Mehta

title: Thoughts from the field; various Buffalo Bills musings from Skarekrow
summary: This week was a bit wacky for me (had a lot of those lately, sorry). I wasn’t able to get anything down to recap the win over the New York Jets before midweek hit but had some various thoughts on things from that game and others as well as the upcoming ones that I felt […]
full_text: This week was a bit wacky for me (had a lot of those lately, sorry). I wasn’t able to get anything down to recap the win over the New York Jets before midweek hit but had some various thoughts on things from that game and others as well as the upcoming ones that I felt might make for good conversation points. And if not, it’ll make for great conversation starters on telling me why I suck. Let’s do it! If you forgot to look at the score, you’d think the Jets had a good game No, seriously. In fact, if you were casually scanning the box score there’s quite a bit of “evidence” that the Jets had as good of a game as the Bills even. That brings me to one of my favorite Skare-isms; The only stat that matters is the score, and everything else is just context. Yes they had the same number of first downs, nearly equal yards, and the Jets even had slightly better third down conversion rate (both teams were lousy), and a significantly higher time of possession. But none of those things win the game. Both teams had eleven drives. The Jets scored on four of them, and the Bills on five. Which again sounds like a close game. How do these stats add context to the only real stat of the “score?” When it mattered, the Jets’ scoring drives ended in field goals. All but one of the Bills’ scoring drives were touchdowns. You put all that context together and that’s how you translate a box score into a blowout. If the Minnesota Vikings had Kirk Cousins against us, I think we lose that game Yeah I know, we blew out the Vikings, how could a middle tier quarterback take a dominant win away from the Buffalo Bills? Well it’s simple, I think Carson Wentz was truly THAT bad against us. Even a mediocre quarterback would have drastically increased their odds. Heck, even a bad quarterback would have significantly increased their odds. And Cousins is a good quarterback. You might point out that we already beat Kirk Cousins once this year against the Las Vegas Raiders. You might also remember he dropped 30 on our defense. Further, we only put up 23 against the Vikings. Now I want to be clear. None of that guarantees a 30 – 23 loss if Cousins was on the Vikings when we played them. Our defense (see below) does seem to be improving and maybe we don’t allow 30 to Cousins. So I can’t definitively say this as anything other than opinion that I think we lose that game against Cousins, but it’s hard to argue they don’t have a much better shot. Is Miami the worst team we’ll face? I’m going to do a deeper dive for my opponent preview but I’ve already taken a preliminary look at the Miami Dolphins’ overall stats. With the point spread at seemingly ludicrous levels for this week I wanted to see if there was reason to think it was… well, reasonable. I think it might be. Based on the heading you might immediately think “Los Angeles Chargers” and that’s not a bad take. Both are now sitting at 1 – 8 and I think we’ve got a pretty good race on our hands. So let’s go to rate metrics as our tiebreaker! On defense, the Chargers rank 17 in points per drive. That’s average by any measure. The Dolphins? They rank 29th which puts them in the “terrible” grouping per my rule of four. Now here’s where the conversation will become divided, and rightfully so. The Dolphins stay put at 29th, or “terrible” in their scoring per drive rate. Not to be outdone though, the Chargers are dead last in scoring output. So which team you taking for the top of the “Crap-O-Meter?” For my money, I stick with my rule of four. With the Chargers having an average defense and Miami scoring terrible on both sides of the ball I gotta go with the Dolphins. If there’s one thing we can all agree on though, is that it’s fun that we have two games against Miami to go. Speaking of the schedule… You gotta play the teams on it and that’s all there is to it. Have the Bills had some lucky breaks this season? Oh god yes. You already know how I feel about being the lucky winner of the “playing against Carson Wentz” sweepstakes. The Ravens should always be taken seriously, except when they’re down to their third string quarterback about 42 seconds into the game. And again, by the end of it we’ll have had three games against teams that are a combined 2 – 16 at the moment. It’s not like the Jets are a juggernaut and we have one more against them, the New England Patriots seem to be stumbling hard (lol), and we’re already at eight wins. Things are looking great for Buffalo and yes, the schedule will almost certainly be a story come season’s end. But opponent fan bases can still bite me if they think I’m going to feel bad about it. We have also the Chicago Bears, the Green Bay Packers, Kansas City, and the Denver Broncos still ahead. We’ve already outgunned two 7 – 2 teams including dropping more points on a superb Vikings defense than anyone and a six-win Los Angeles Rams team. Honestly, our schedule is a pretty mixed bag with only a few teams I’d put in the “meh” category. So sure, we’ll stack some wins against the dregs but we’ve been also shown up against the elites. Which brings me to… Are we serious about a Super Bowl run? I think we should be as serious as we have been for a few years now. Yeah, I’m worried about the defense. I was worried LAST year and there’s no objective argument to currently say that we’re in better shape on that side of the ball this year. We COULD be by the end of it with Amani Hooker sliding right in and hopefully the entire team playing a bit more comfortably as the weeks roll by. And like I said above, there’s no one we CAN’T beat. NO ONE! I’m not claiming unbeatable. There are games that have me worried. There are teams that have me worried. I’m not so worried that I plan on going into a game all doom and gloom though. Further, I’ve already hinted at this but we have a shot at the one seed. Matt Warren’s already made content to this effect but if we take care of the games we should at the moment that puts us at a 12-win season (Jets, Pats, Miami x 2). That leaves us with four games that aren’t “should win” but are also not “should lose” aka “could win.” Splitting those is a 14-win season and that’s a great shot at the one seed. Now the competition is tight with a staggering four teams only a game behind us. Two of which can get a head-to-head win over us during our Holiday jaunts (Kansas City and Denver). That’s not ideal, but only if THEY get the win. If we get the head-to-head win that’s 100% ideal. Realistically we just need to keep pace in wins to take it and there’s some good news. Kansas City has to face not just us but the Cincinnati Bengals (see below), the Rams, and the San Franciso 49ers so they don’t have easy sledding either. The Bengals are also one game behind us with the aforementioned game against Kansas City and two games against the six-win Cleveland Browns. Jacksonville might be a little more of a worry with games against the Bears and Pittsburgh Steelers the biggest obstacles. If they go on a run they could be trouble. Denver might be the biggest concern again this year and winning on Christmas would be huge for the Bills. The Broncos have games against the Steelers and us. They need to play the Raiders twice and they’ve been plucky at times but just traded away their quarterback. Making them a bigger concern for our one seed shot is that the Denver Broncos have that same nagging “schedule” complaint that fans are lobbing at us. Games against the Jets, Dolphins, and Chargers should be wins. So what do I see? A prediction would be a nice way to wrap up an article like this one I think. I don’t see a reason the Bills don’t win the games they should win. I won’t be so specific as to say which games for all four, but I really like our chances against Denver, and I’ll call that a win and at least one more of the tougher ones. Bills go at least 14 – 3 in my opinion.
author: Skarekrow

title: A study on the impact of Josh Allen’s interceptions
summary: Josh Allen is universally regarded as an elite NFL quarterback, but that doesn’t mean he’s immune to criticism. And when Allen criticism arises, it tends to be centered around his interceptions. From his breakout 2020 campaign through 2023, Allen reached double digits in the interception category each year. After only six in 2024’s MVP season, […]
full_text: Josh Allen is universally regarded as an elite NFL quarterback, but that doesn’t mean he’s immune to criticism. And when Allen criticism arises, it tends to be centered around his interceptions. From his breakout 2020 campaign through 2023, Allen reached double digits in the interception category each year. After only six in 2024’s MVP season, Allen tossed 10 a season ago and already has seven in nine games in 2026. If obtaining a doctoral in football analysis was possible, I would write my dissertation on why we can’t view interceptions in a vacuum and their presence as a necessary byproduct of properly aggressive quarterback play. And a lot more things to challenge conventional wisdom about picks from a quarterback in the NFL. That is not the objective of this article. But it’s related to that. The point here is to demonstrate how Allen’s interceptions are unique. He’s become a master of the arm-punt pick, a worst-case result on a play in which a seismic chance is made in search of a hugely positive play for the offense. And the worst-case result of the arm punt is the least damaging in the grand scheme of all possible interceptions. Shoutout to WGR 550’s Jeremy White for noticing / highlighting this trend a while ago, by the way. Since 2020, Allen has lost an average of 3.76 Expected Points Added on interceptions, the third-lowest average among qualifying quarterbacks. (naturally, all interceptions create negative EPA for the offense). The two quarterbacks ahead of him — meaning less EPA lost, on average — are 2024 draftees, Caleb Williams (3.74 lost), and Bo Nix at (3.60). This season, through Week 10, Allen has lost an average of 2.78 EPA on his seven interceptions, the third-lowest among the 35 quarterbacks with at least 100 pass attempts on the season. The second-lowest currently is J.J. McCarthy at 2.50 EPA lost on interceptions. Lamar Jackson only lost 1.78 EPA on his lone interception to date this season. Those 2026 Allen interceptions have happened on: 1st and 20 2nd and 7 2nd and 6 3rd and 6 1st and 10 3rd and 23 3rd and 12 And five of the seven occurred on throws made 20 or more air yards down the field. Since 2020, 33.8% of Allen’s interceptions have come on those deep throws (20+ air yards), a rate higher than Lamar Jackson (29.2%), Joe Burrow (22.8%) and Patrick Mahomes (22.5%). When it comes to interceptions thrown on 3rd and 10+ situations, on fourth down, or on deep throws, 41.3% of his interceptions since the start of 2020 meet at least one of those requirements. That’s a higher rate than Jackson (35.4%), Burrow (31.6%), and Mahomes (29.6%). Of course, Allen — or any quarterback for that matter — essentially has little to no impact on the return that occurs on his interceptions. But this season and throughout his career post-breakout, the picks Allen takes heat for have been among the least damaging by EPA. That’s uniquely captivating, isn’t it? I’d be insane to suggest Allen is deliberately throwing interceptions with the prescience of knowing they’ll be minimally detrimental. This just is what it is. And no interception represents an ideal result for an offense, of course. But the frequency of Allen’s interceptions occurring in unfavorable down-and-distance scenarios and on long throws have mitigated their negative impact on the Bills in a given game and suggest there’s something distinctive about the risks he takes.
author: Chris Trapasso

title: Buffalo Bills’ first injury report of Week 11 brings bad news to secondary
summary: There were a couple of surprises on the Buffalo Bills’ first injury report of Week 11, with the team beginning practice on Wednesday for Sunday’s game against the Miami Dolphins.  None of the starting offensive linemen were sidelined today. Well, that’s not entirely accurate — right guard O’Cyrus Torrence, the only lineman not dealing with an […]
full_text: There were a couple of surprises on the Buffalo Bills’ first injury report of Week 11, with the team beginning practice on Wednesday for Sunday’s game against the Miami Dolphins. None of the starting offensive linemen were sidelined today. Well, that’s not entirely accurate — right guard O’Cyrus Torrence, the only lineman not dealing with an injury last week, was on Wednesday’s report, but for personal reasons rather than an injury. But the rest of the surprises on today’s report? They weren’t of the fun variety. Wednesday injury report pic.twitter.com/gVDIeno9Ij — Buffalo Bills PR (@BuffaloBillsPR) November 18, 2026 Did Not Practice CB Dee Alford CB Christian Benford TE Dalton Kincaid OG O’Cyrus Torrence LB Dorian Williams None of these are particularly surprising. Maybe Kincaid. The Bills’ top tight end seems to be playing some version of “Spin the Wheel” when it comes to injuries this season. Weeks 8 and 9, it was a chest injury. Last week, it was an ankle. Now he’s keeping the ankle ailment and adding a thumb injury to go with it for Week 11. Otherwise, these injuries were evident during Sunday’s game, so it’s no surprise that any of the players listed here are getting another day — or three — off. Limited Practice S Cole Bishop RB Ray Davis S Damar Hamlin S Amani Hooker Here, we have the group that decided to surprise this week. None of them were on last week’s injury list, so the injuries all came during or after Sunday’s game at MetLife Stadium. That turf is unforgiving, but not all of these may have happened on game day. We did see Hooker coming out of the medical tent Sunday, but never got any confirmation from the Bills as to why. Now we know it had something to do with his knee. We saw Bishop getting attention from trainers on the sideline. He was seen wincing as they manipulated his arm. It’s Hamlin that gives us reason to pause. It’s not great that the Bills have three injured safeties. Plus Hamlin has spent significant snaps replacing Alford, who’s dealing with a concussion right now, at nickel. Sal Capaccio with WGR550 reported seeing Hamlin in a boot and using a scooter at the end of practice. That, information — along with a limited designation — would indicate Hamlin started practice healthy. An in-practice injury that puts him in an immobilizer is not a good sign that Hamlin will play on Sunday. Saw Damar Hamlin walking with a scooter and boot on his right foot after today’s practice. — Sal Capaccio 🏈 (@SalSports) November 18, 2026 Full Practice WR Keon Coleman RB Ty Johnson C Connor McGovern DL T.J. Sanders WR Tyrell Shavers The big news here is Shavers. Head coach Joe Brady announced before practice that the team was moving Shavers to the active roster. Shavers started the season on PUP after tearing his ACL in playoff action against the Jacksonville Jaguars this past January. Joe Brady says the #Bills are activating Tyrell Shavers off of injured reserve. — Jon Scott (@JonScottTV) November 18, 2026 What We’re Watching The Bills thought they solved their defensive back problem. They cut C.J. Gardner-Johnson, signed Amani Hooker, got Dee Alford back from an injury, discovered versatility in Damar Hamlin, and found that rookie Davison Igbinosun was doing well at boundary corner. Now they’re suddenly facing a shortage once again. Hamlin and Christian Benford aren’t a lock to play Sunday. Alford has to work through the league’s concussion protocol. And, if they do play, Bishop and Hooker may not be full speed. The current uninjured Buffalo secondary would look like Jordan Hancock at NCB, Sam Franklin, Jr. and Jalon Kilgore at safety; Maxwell Hairston and Igbinosun on the boundaries. The answer may just be a veteran. Today, Brady said that Tre’Davious White was brought in to help this team win. On Monday, defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard said that he feels White is ready to step up if needed. With Christian Benford and Maxwell Hairston banged up after the Jets game, Bills DC Jim Leonhard said he likes where Tre'Davious White is at as he's ramped up conditioning over the past few weeks. "If need be, I think he's ready to step up and help us." pic.twitter.com/piNAcVWFsZ — Matt Parrino (@MattParrino) November 16, 2026 Today’s memo seems to be: Needed.

title: Buffalo Bills Week 10 snap counts: Defensive rotation and injuries stand out in win over Jets
summary: The Buffalo Bills improved their position in the AFC East with a 31-12 victory over the New York Jets at MetLife Stadium on Sunday Buffalo’s offense played just 57 snaps compared to 71 for the defense. The Jets held a 32:01 to 27:59 advantage in time of possession, but Buffalo made its opportunities count, producing […]
full_text: The Buffalo Bills improved their position in the AFC East with a 31-12 victory over the New York Jets at MetLife Stadium on Sunday Buffalo’s offense played just 57 snaps compared to 71 for the defense. The Jets held a 32:01 to 27:59 advantage in time of possession, but Buffalo made its opportunities count, producing 389 total yards and four touchdowns. While the Jets finished with a 32:01 to 27:59 advantage in time of possession, that statistic doesn’t tell the entire story. Buffalo actually controlled the clock in the first half, holding the ball for 18:36 compared to New York’s 11:24. The second half was a different story, largely because the Bills’ offense simply didn’t need much time to score. Buffalo produced three touchdown drives totaling just seven offensive plays and 2:49 of possession. Josh Allen capped a four-play drive with a rushing touchdown, connected with DJ Moore on a 45-yard score during a two-play possession, and James Cook put the game away with a 74-yard touchdown run on the first play of another drive. Those three possessions accounted for 21 points in less than three minutes. The defense certainly had its share of extended drives to contend with, but Buffalo’s explosive offensive production played a significant role in the disparity between offensive and defensive snap counts. Offensive snap counts The Bills’ offensive line remained relatively consistent throughout the afternoon. Left tackle Dion Dawkins and right guard O’Cyrus Torrence played all 57 snaps, while Connor McGovern, Alec Anderson, and Spencer Brown each played 54 (95%). Josh Allen also played 54 snaps before Kyle Allen entered for the final three plays. At running back, James Cook led the group with 35 snaps (61%), followed by Ray Davis with 12 (21%) and Ty Johnson with 10 (18%). Cook made the most of his opportunities, rushing for 157 yards and a touchdown on 18 carries, including a 74-yard scoring run in the fourth quarter. The wide receiver rotation was more evenly distributed. Khalil Shakir led the group with 36 snaps (63%), followed by DJ Moore with 33 (58%), Keon Coleman with 30 (53%), and Skyler Bell with 20 (35%). The tight end usage was particularly interesting. Dawson Knox led the position with 41 snaps (72%), while Jackson Hawes and Dalton Kincaid each played 26 (46%). Keleki Latu contributed another 13 snaps (23%). Defensive snap counts Safety Amani Hooker played every defensive snap, while Cole Bishop played 68 (96%). Cornerback Davison Igbinosun was on the field for 66 snaps (93%), making him one of the defense’s most heavily utilized players. Christian Benford played 53 snaps (75%), while Dee Alford played just 20 (28%). Both were listed as out of the game in the fourth quarter, contributing to additional opportunities for Maxwell Hairston, who played 23 snaps (32%), and Jordan Hancock, who played 35 (49%). At linebacker, Terrel Bernard led the group with 60 snaps (85%). Dorian Williams played 32 (45%) and Kaleb Elarms-Orr played 25 (35%). The defensive front continued to rotate personnel. Deone Walker and Ed Oliver each played 47 snaps (66%), while Greg Rousseau and Bradley Chubb each played 42 (59%). One of the more notable performances came from T.J. Parker, who played 39 snaps (55%) and recorded two sacks, three quarterback hits, and two tackles for loss. Michael Hoecht played just 11 defensive snaps (15%) but still contributed a sack, while Javon Solomon played 12 (17%) and forced a fourth-quarter fumble that helped seal the victory. Special teams Special teams participation was led by Joe Andreessen and Sam Franklin, who each played 22 snaps (81%). Latu and Solomon each contributed 18 special teams snaps (67%), while Hancock, Hamlin, and Hoecht each played 17 (63%). Observations Offensively, the Bills struggled on third down, converting just two of 10 opportunities, but explosive plays from Cook, Moore, and Kincaid helped compensate for those shortcomings. Perhaps the biggest takeaway from this week’s snap counts is the workload placed on Buffalo’s secondary. With Benford and Alford leaving the game, the Bills relied on their depth to finish the afternoon. Buffalo will need to monitor those injuries heading into Week 11, but the defensive rotation and timely playmaking were enough to secure another divisional victory.

Shavers, 27, burst onto the scene in 2025 playing 38% of the snaps after hardly seeing the field in his first two […]
full_text: There’s been a development in the Buffalo Bills wide receiver room — Tyrell Shavers is set to make his 2026 debut after tearing his ACL in the wild-card win in Jacksonville last January. Joe Brady says the #Bills are activating Tyrell Shavers off of injured reserve. — Jon Scott (@JonScottTV) November 18, 2026 Shavers, 27, burst onto the scene in 2025 playing 38% of the snaps after hardly seeing the field in his first two seasons with the Bills. In Week 11 against the Buccaneers, he had four catches for 90 yards and a touchdown. Shavers blocked on 232 run plays a season ago as well. While not especially thick-framed, the former Alabama and San Diego State wideout is sizable at 6’4” and 211 pounds. Shavers will be added to the 53-man roster. Ar’maj Reed-Adams being played on IR Tuesday made room for this move. We’ll see if Shavers, now 10 months removed from his ACL tear, is quickly inserted into the receiver rotation within Josh Allen’s offense as early as Sunday against the Dolphins.

title: Buffalo Bills trending up, trending down: Bills beat Jets, and Dolphins come next
summary: The Buffalo Bills beat the New York Jets 31-12, and the defense that closed the game deserves most of the credit. With a second divisional matchup in sight, Miami is 1-8 and has lost three straight, and Buffalo is favored by 16.5 according to SI’s betting preview. The record hides a defense that has allowed […]
full_text: The Buffalo Bills beat the New York Jets 31-12, and the defense that closed the game deserves most of the credit. With a second divisional matchup in sight, Miami is 1-8 and has lost three straight, and Buffalo is favored by 16.5 according to SI’s betting preview. The record hides a defense that has allowed 320.5 yards per game, the 10th fewest in the NFL, while facing one of the toughest schedules of opposing offenses. That is the group the Bills will see on Sunday, and here are the players who can make the difference for Buffalo: Keep It Up T.J. Parker, outside linebacker Parker had two sacks on consecutive plays early in the fourth quarter and five pressures on 26 pass-rush snaps, per PFF. He is the first Bills rookie with two or more sacks in a game since Greg Rousseau did it against Miami in 2021, and he now has 3.5 on the season. He played more than half the defensive snaps and made the most of his opportunities. Miami’s line has given up 24 sacks on Malik Willis, and in Week 10 the Colts credited 8 pressures and 3 sacks on Kyle McCord, who was making his first NFL start. With McCord most likely under center again, a fast rusher who wins early is exactly the problem he does not want. DJ Moore, wide receiver Moore finished with four catches for 90 yards and a 45-yard touchdown, plus a 32-yard catch on a crossing route. His 75.1 PFF grade was one of the five best on offense. The Dolphins play rookies at a higher rate than any defense in the league, and cornerback Chris Johnson and safety Michael Taaffe have played every defensive snap since Week 7. Taaffe has three interceptions, and Johnson returned one for a 59-yard touchdown against Indianapolis. A veteran who finds space against young defensive backs is what Buffalo needs against a ball-hawking secondary. Moore should find opportunities to haul in another big play or two if Joe Brady gives him the opportunity to capitalize deep again. Terrel Bernard, linebacker After taking heavy criticism following a rough 2025 season (48.8 PFF grade, 73rd of 88 linebackers) and a 39.9 grade in Week 5, Terrel Bernard deserves real credit for his recent turnaround. Over the last two weeks, he has totaled 14 tackles, two passes defended, an interception, and zero missed tackles against the Jets — highlighted by a 72.5 PFF grade in Week 10 and a massive, clean hit that knocked Geno Smith out of the game. That surge has boosted his season grade to 66.6 (29th of 82) with a 65.0 coverage mark and an 80.9 passer rating allowed. Buffalo will need that version of Bernard on Sunday to anchor the middle against Miami’s Ollie Gordon II — who just posted 100 yards against Minnesota and 88 against Cincinnati — and contain quarterback Kyle McCord (17-of-32, 209 yards vs. Indianapolis), who thrives on quick, underneath throws. Step Up James Cook, running back (In the passing game ) Hear me out. Cook ran for 157 yards at 8.7 per carry against the Jets, and the run game is not the issue. The receiving side is. Through Week 10, he has 12 catches on 19 targets for 110 yards, with two drops according to Pro Football Reference, and an average depth of target of -0.2 yards. In Week 9, he failed to bring in his only target against Minnesota. Josh Allen said publicly that he needs to take more checkdowns, but we know that’s not his favorite kind of throw. When he decides to settle for it, seeing his running back not getting the job done makes that harder. Cook is leaving receiving production on the table in a role that fits him. This offense can be way more dangerous if he can take advantage of those more often. Honorable Mentions Keep It Up Khalil Shakir, wide receiver: The highest PFF grade on the offense (77.6) came on two catches for 26 yards, three rushes for 29, and an 80.3 blocking grade. His short-game work is what to watch against a young secondary that tackles well. Spencer Brown, right tackle: Brown did not practice early in the week and was doubtful, yet played and allowed no pressures on 13 reps against Jets rookie David Bailey, per Next Gen Stats. Bailey came into the game with 40 pressures on 194 pass-rush attempts (20.6%). His PFF grade was 75.3. Chop Robinson is a different test, but Brown showed he can handle a top young rusher. Dalton Kincaid, tight end: His 54-yard catch started the second half, and he earned a 73.1 PFF grade. Miami’s rookie linebacker Jacob Rodriguez has played 99.3 percent of the defensive snaps, using Kincaid over the middle is a matchup to test the rookie in coverage. Step Up Dawson Knox, tight end: One catch for 7 yards on three targets, a 41.2 PFF grade (the lowest of any offensive player on the team) and a 51.1 run-blocking grade. His best game of the year came a week earlier: four catches on five targets for 37 yards. Buffalo needs that level of play against Miami’s linebackers. T.J. Sanders, defensive tackle: A 39.6 PFF grade. Miami has leaned on Gordon, so the interior has to hold up. After a promising start to his season, he hasn’t played well as his role diminished with Ed Oliver back. Jordan Hancock, cornerback: A 43.7 PFF grade. With Christian Benford, Max Hairston, and Dee Alford banged up, more of the secondary will fall on him. He has to make the most of his opportunities, especially with how well Te’Cory Couch played in his last game. Final Thoughts The Jets game showed a defense that punishes opposing QBs and an offense that was grounded for most of the first half, but had an extra gear to make up for it in the second. Miami, 1-8 and starting a rookie quarterback, is the kind of opponent that they can’t allow to give them trouble. Parker, Moore, and Bernard have the best case to build on Sunday, and Cook and Chubb have the clearest chance to change the story. Which of this week’s Step Up names do you think responds best against Miami? Catch up on all this and more with the latest edition of Leading the Charge!

title: Examining Buffalo Bills run heaviness in first half of 2026 season
summary: The Buffalo Bills have loved running the football thus far in the 2026 season. James Cook has the second-most carries in the NFL right now at 187. As a team, the Bills are the current owners of the second-highest first-down designed run rate in the NFL at 61.3%. Now, sure, the Bills have recently played […]
full_text: The Buffalo Bills have loved running the football thus far in the 2026 season. James Cook has the second-most carries in the NFL right now at 187. As a team, the Bills are the current owners of the second-highest first-down designed run rate in the NFL at 61.3%. Now, sure, the Bills have recently played in a collection of games that featured plenty of garbage time, when Buffalo has attempted to burn clock by tapping into the run game. Even when garbage-time is considered, the Bills have the NFL’s second-highest run rate on all downs at 45.7%. The rest of the league averages a designed run play on 39.3%. Quarterback scrambles — that occur on dropbacks — and spikes and kneels are excluded in that calculation. Analytics have proven that passing the football is more efficient than running the football. And this article isn’t going to show that the Bills have actually become more efficient on the ground than through the air. Right now, in non-garbage time situations, Buffalo’s designed-run game has provided the team +0.023 EPA per play, the eighth-highest figure in the NFL. The team’s pass game has provided the team +0.239 EPA per dropback, the fourth-best in football. Unsurprisingly, the difference in value added for each method of moving the football has been seismic. Up until now, the Bills have genuinely attempted to “establish” the run in their first nine games of the 2026 campaign. Accepting that fact raises two questions: what type of play call have the Bills chosen on second down and how effective have their second downs been? Before I begin with the results, despite an overall negative EPA in first-down run scenarios (-0.059, the 15th-highest in football), the Bills have had 16.4% of those runs gain 10+ yards. That’s the fourth-best in the NFL and much higher than the league average of 10.3%. This is where things get fascinating for Buffalo’s elite offense. And where it has leaned on its pass game. On second down after a first-down run — in non-garbage time scenarios, of course — the Bills have dropped back to pass 73.8% of the time, which is the fourth-highest rate in the NFL and noticeably higher than the league average of 64.5%. On all second downs, regardless of whether a run or pass was called on first down, the Bills’ dropback rate is 66.9%, the ninth-highest in the NFL. While the Bills are actually below league average in conventional passing statistics within both second-down parameters, they are 12th in EPA per dropback in second downs after a first down run and on all non-garbage time second downs. An enormous element of said impressive EPA per dropback on second down for the Bills despite below-average passing statistics in those situations is of course Josh Allen scrambles, the ultimately luxury built into Buffalo’s dropback game. The possibility of an Allen scramble occurring on a dropback must be considered. Allen has eight scrambles on second-down runs that have totaled 87 yards. That’s 10.9 yards per scramble, the second-highest average among all quarterbacks in those scenarios. His +1.162 EPA on those plays, is far and away, tops in the NFL. You have survived this massive number dump, and I appreciate you making it this far. Essentially, yes — the Bills have been very run heavy. But they’ve smartly morphed into being one of the league’s more pass-happy clubs on second down, and Allen’s running on second-down dropbacks have been incredibly effective.

title: Buffalo Bills recent adds to roster have provided value
summary: Sometimes, important additions to an NFL team don’t occur until close to September… or even in-season. On August 18, after their first preseason game, the Bills signed veteran defensive lineman Greg Gaines — potentially as a response to rookie defensive tackle Zane Durant being injured late in the opening exhibition game against the Panthers. Almost […]
full_text: Sometimes, important additions to an NFL team don’t occur until close to September… or even in-season. On August 18, after their first preseason game, the Bills signed veteran defensive lineman Greg Gaines — potentially as a response to rookie defensive tackle Zane Durant being injured late in the opening exhibition game against the Panthers. Almost exactly two weeks later, on the last day of August, as the team seemingly had no clear-cut candidate to return punts, Buffalo scooped up Greg Dortch after he was surprisingly cut by the Lions. Through the first nine games of the season, both have provided valuable, low-key contributions to this Bills team. On the surface, Gaines’ presence has been irrelevant. He has 11 tackles and one tackles for loss along with two pressures on 77 pass-rush snaps on 22.5% of Buffalo’s defensive snaps. But when Gaines is on the field, he’s a magnet for blockers, which has a massive ripple effect on his teammates. More blockers on him, fewer on other Bills defenders. Gaines is currently 10th in the NFL among qualifying defensive linemen in double-team rate (67.5%) on pass-rush snaps. It’s the highest rate on Buffalo’s roster right now (among qualifiers). As for Dortch, the value he’s added has been easier to discern. Among punt returners with at least 15 returns to date, his 9.2 yards-per-return average is seventh-best in the NFL. He’s been darn good as a kicker returner too, so teams aren’t able to simply directionally kick it away from reigning All-Pro kicker returner Ray Davis. While Davis is second in the NFL in average kick-return yardage at 29.6 entering Week 11, Dortch is tied for 12th with an average of 27.2 yards per kick return. And he’s actually returned nearly double the amount of kickoffs (23) as Davis (12). And then there’s Amani Hooker. Of course, the jury is still out on how much the trade-deadline acquisition will impact Buffalo’s defense. But in his first game, after a week of practice in a new scheme on a new team, he played the most defensive snaps of any Bills defender (70), made seven tackles, and had a pass breakup that was nearly an interception. Hooker will play a full-time role at free safety the rest of the way. Gaines and Dortch have proven to be savvy, low-cost additions by the Bills close to the start of the regular season. These adds have become the embodiment of Brandon Beane’s often cited perpetual pursuit of improving the roster.

title: Carolina Panthers 2027 NFL Draft Prospect Profile: David Olano
summary: The 2027 NFL Draft feels like forever away, and we’re all caught up in the NFL season. Regardless, it’s never too early to look ahead to the Draft. This twice weekly series will take a closer look at some of the prospects the Carolina Panthers could select in the 2027 iteration of the Draft. In […]
full_text: COLLEGE STATION, TEXAS - SEPTEMBER 12: David Olano #24 of the Texas A&M Aggies kicks a field goal in the second half Arizona State Sun Devils at Kyle Field on September 12, 2026 in College Station, Texas. (Photo by Tim Warner/Getty Images) | Getty Images The 2027 NFL Draft feels like forever away, and we’re all caught up in the NFL season. Regardless, it’s never too early to look ahead to the Draft. This twice weekly series will take a closer look at some of the prospects the Carolina Panthers could select in the 2027 iteration of the Draft. In this series, we’ll only be looking at prospects the Panthers could seriously consider. Today our profile will focus on Texas A&M Aggies kicker David Olano. Bio Olano (5’10”, 160 lbs.) was originally a three star recruit out of Naperville, IL. He spent his first three collegiate seasons with the home state Illini, taking over the full time kicker role his sophomore season. During his two on-field seasons with Illinois, Olano made 37 of 43 field goal attempts while going 82/83 on extra points. That resume earned him an offer from Texas A&M, and he transferred to the bigger stage. He has been just as good so far this season, nailing 16 of 18 field goals (including 4/5 from 50+ yards) and making all 27 extra point attempts. Strengths/Weaknesses Olano is an ultra reliable kicker, especially in the mid range. He’s shown the ability to hit longer kicks this season, including a career long 57 yarder against Arkansas. His leg strength has shown on kickoffs as well, getting a touchback on 87% of his kickoffs, up from a sub-70% mark for his career at Illinois. Olano also has a hanful of clutch kicks on his resume, including a couple walk-off winners in 2025. He has good trajectory and lift on his field goal attempts, only having two career kicks blocked. Olano has a strong enough leg to be effective at the next level, but he doesn’t have the “nuclear” leg of someone like Cam Little. There are also some concerns this year about his fatigue. He missed a field goal in two consecutive games after starting the season out 16/16, so some scouts are concerned about his ability to make it through a 17 game season without splitting kickoff duties. As with most college kickers, the change in NFL kickoff rules makes them tough to project in that area of the game. Kickoffs are not preferred in the NFL like they are in college, so Olano’s ability to drop kicks inside the landing zone is untested. Projection Olano has the precision from every distance that NFL teams covet. He has enough leg to consistently hit from 50+, though the longer 60+ yard kicks might be out of his range. He is consistent year over year, making over 85% of his field goal attempts every season in college. His lack of a monster leg and unproven directional kickoffs might push him toward the end of Day 3 of the Draft or potentially out of the Draft altogether. The Carolina Panthers don’t normally use draft capital on kickers (the only kicker drafted by the team was almost ten years ago when they took Harrison Butker). However, Ryan Fitzgerald’s sophomore slump has caused some concern among fans. Dave Canales has publicly backed Fitz, but if his struggles continue the team could look to upgrade the position. What do you think, Panthers fans? If David Olano is available when the Panthers select in the 2027 NFL Draft, should they take him? Sound off in the comments!
