title: The 2026 Packers are what wasting a quarterback looks like
summary: For most of a decade, you couldn’t escape takes implying the Packers were somehow wasting Aaron Rodgers. Here was a preternaturally talented quarterback, perhaps the most gifted we’ve ever seen, and he can’t make it back to the Super Bowl. Who do we blame for that, both fans and media folks wondered loudly and often. […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - NOVEMBER 15: Levi Drake Rodriguez #50 of the Minnesota Vikings sacks Jordan Love #10 of the Green Bay Packers during the second quarter at Lambeau Field on November 15, 2026 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Michael Reaves/Getty Images) | Getty Images For most of a decade, you couldn’t escape takes implying the Packers were somehow wasting Aaron Rodgers. Here was a preternaturally talented quarterback, perhaps the most gifted we’ve ever seen, and he can’t make it back to the Super Bowl. Who do we blame for that, both fans and media folks wondered loudly and often. The substance of those complaints centered on the Packers’ reluctance to sign outside free agents. But despite that reticence, the Packers still made plenty of deep playoff runs under Aaron Rodgers. Change maybe a dozen plays across the span of 10 years or so and you could probably send the Packers to three or four more Super Bowls. They were that close and that frequently in the mix, even without regular forays into free agency. I’ve never been a big fan of the “wasting Aaron Rodgers’ prime” discussion, mostly because of how unfalsifiable so many of the alternatives were. What free agents and for how much? How do we really know they’d have made a difference? Brandon Bostick still dropped the onside kick in the 2014 NFC Championship even as Julius Peppers, the Packers’ biggest free agent signing post-Charles Woodson, watched from the sideline. But if we concede there was anything at all to the idea of squandering Rodgers, what the Packers have done this season with Jordan Love is orders of magnitude worse. Firmly in a “we’re going for it!” championship window after their aggressive move to acquire Micah Parsons, the Packers have fielded a half dozen different variations of a completely unplayable offensive line. The line is beyond non-functioning. It’s a wasteland of talentlessness. To be sure, injuries have played a factor in that reality. They’re without Zach Bako-Bewele now and possibly forever, but even if Bako-Bewele was healthy, the interior offensive line would still be bereft of talent. Aaron Banks would still be an expensive albatross at left guard. Anthony Belton might have been able to muddle his way through at right guard, but that’s no guarantee. Sean Rhyan would still be injured, but even if he weren’t, the Packers’ depth would be a travesty. Even at their healthiest, they’d be just an injury or two from being right where they are now. The Packers’ defense is good enough to win a Super Bowl. Micah Parsons is returning to a unit that’s proven it can get the job done, and that’s even without playmaker Edgerrin Cooper and veteran presence Javon Hargrave. They’ve added enough pieces to make this defense more than good enough. And outside of the offensive line, the rest of the offense has been exceptional. Christian Watson and Matthew Golden are as good a pair of receivers as you could ask for. Tucker Kraft, even in his diminished state, is a noteworthy tight end. The running backs…okay, you’ve got me there, but even the Packers pathetic running backs would look better behind a capable offensive line. Kaleb Johnson has enough juice to find a few holes, and if they appeared more regularly, you have to think he’d be capable enough to find them. And we haven’t even mentioned Love himself. Our colleagues around the NFC North may not agree that he’s a great quarterback (he is), but I’d think even the most steadfast Bears fan would concede Love is hardly getting a fair shake this year. They might even be generous enough to say he’s doing quite well, given the circumstances. But those circumstances are reprehensible. The Packers’ handling of the offensive line both prior to and during this massively important season has been completely unserious. Their best efforts to fix their self-inflicted problems have been to sign Laken Tomlinson off the Cowboys’ practice squad, add Mekhi Becton off the street, and hope that Kevin Zeitler’s surgically repaired 36-year-old body could hold up to a sudden return to football. Tomlinson and Becton have so far showed exactly why they were available, and Zeitler has played the part of an old warhorse on his last legs. Which is to say, he probably should have stayed out to pasture, but who can blame him? I’d take quite a few lumps for a couple of million dollars, too. It’s not the players’ fault, though. It’s the supposed adults in the room that thought this would be good enough that deserve the blame. And if we had to sit through years of people accusing the Packers of wasting Aaron Rodgers, we’d do well to crank up the heat when the Packers are actually wasting their quarterback.

title: The Packers have one of the hardest NFL schedules to end 2026
summary: According to ESPN’s Football Power Index (FPI), the Green Bay Packers have played an average-ish NFL schedule this season, as they’re ranked 16th in strength of schedule league-wide. Coming out of the bye, though, their slate will get a lot tougher leading up to the postseason. Per FPI, the Packers have the fifth-hardest schedule in […]
full_text: (Photo by Sean M. Haffey/Getty Images) | Getty Images According to ESPN’s Football Power Index (FPI), the Green Bay Packers have played an average-ish NFL schedule this season, as they’re ranked 16th in strength of schedule league-wide. Coming out of the bye, though, their slate will get a lot tougher leading up to the postseason. Per FPI, the Packers have the fifth-hardest schedule in the league moving forward, only behind the Los Angeles Rams, Seattle Seahawks, Miami Dolphins and Kansas City Chiefs. For perspective, the other NFC North teams rank sixth (Chicago Bears), 16th (Detroit Lions) and 22nd (Minnesota Vikings). Moving forward, this is the Packers’ schedule: Week 12: @ Los Angeles Rams Week 13: @ New Orleans Saints Week 14: vs. Buffalo Bills Week 15: vs. Miami Dolphins Week 16: @ Chicago Bears Week 17: vs. Houston Texans Week 18: vs. Detroit Lions At the moment, Green Bay sits in the seventh spot in the NFC playoff race with a 6-4 record, a three-way tie in which the Packers hold an advantage over the Seahawks and the Rams. Currently, Green Bay has a 37 percent playoff chance, according to The Athletic’s playoff simulator , but a lot will change based on their upcoming game in Los Angeles. If the Packers win that game, their playoff chances jump up to 59 percent. If they lose, they will drop to 24 percent. That’s a huge amount of playoff leverage, because Green Bay is fighting to hold onto that seventh seed against a team with the same record. For reference, here’s the current playoff leverage in each of the Packers’ remaining games, in isolation, going into Week 11’s action: Rams: 35 percent Saints: 23 percent Bills: 21 percent Dolphins: 19 percent Bears: 34 percent Texans: 19 percent Lions: 30 percent Yes, the Rams game means more than the two divisional games left on their schedule, mostly because the simulations only give the Packers a one percent chance to win the division at this point. Being 6-4 in mid-November in one of the toughest divisions in NFL history will do that. Against non-division opponents, the NFC North is 21-4 this season, an 84 percent win percentage. The best mark for a division in NFL history was the 1984 AFC West, which posted a 78 percent mark. For what it’s worth, the best all-time full-season division in NFC history was the 2024 NFC North, when they collectively won 75 percent of their non-division games. Even compared to 2024, the 2026 North is a step ahead. The Packers still control their own destiny, but this upcoming Rams game is a cornerstone to that path. If they end up losing to Los Angeles, they’re going to need some help to get into the postseason — even as a wild-card team. On top of that, they’ll need to make up that distance while playing one of the toughest schedules in the league. Things are shaping up for a very competitive race for a playoff spot between the Rams, Seahawks and Packers, who all have top-five schedules coming out of their Week 11 byes.

title: Why is Luke Butkus exempt from public criticism?
summary: Matt LaFleur has no problem criticizing the offensive line. He has no problems saying there are issues with how the offensive line is coached. He, like everyone else, knows the offensive line is a problem. So why is his offensive line coach exempt from criticism? Bring up the name Luke Butkus and suddenly the offensive […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, IN - AUGUST 16: Green Bay Packers Offensive Line Coach Luke Butkus looks on before the NFL preseason game between the Green Bay Packers and the Indianapolis Colts on August 16, 2025, at Lucas Oil Stadium in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Michael Allio/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Matt LaFleur has no problem criticizing the offensive line. He has no problems saying there are issues with how the offensive line is coached. He, like everyone else, knows the offensive line is a problem. So why is his offensive line coach exempt from criticism? Bring up the name Luke Butkus and suddenly the offensive line picture is rosy. “He was the same guy when we were rolling,” LaFleur said of Butkus after the Packers’ latest offensive line collapse. “I think it’s easy to pinpoint and point the finger, and everybody wants to pinpoint blame, but the blame can go to everybody. So it’s all of us in this together. Certainly it starts with myself, and then it goes to everybody else, and it’s coaches and players collectively.” According to LaFleur, then, it’s not Butkus’s fault, but it also is his fault, and it’s the players’ fault, and it’s the other coaches’ fault, and possibly the general manager’s fault. It might also be your fault, which is something I hadn’t considered before. I’ve been spending Packers’ gamedays just watching their offensive line get shredded and never once have I tried to do anything about it. I’m sorry. It starts with me. But why can’t Butkus be criticized? Why is it impossible that he’s part of the problem? I understand that LaFleur isn’t going to stand at the lectern and blast one of his coaches any more than he’s going to single out an individual player for post-loss criticism delivered through the media, but it’s insulting to our collective football intelligence that he won’t even entertain the question. That’s not hyperbole, lest we forget. After an embarrassing Thursday Night Football loss to the Atlanta Falcons earlier this year, reporters brought Luke Butkus up as a possible reason for the poor offensive line performance. LaFleur said “I’m not even going to respond to that.” Why? LaFleur is more than willing to criticize the coaching obliquely. After the Packers’ Week 1 collapse LaFleur said he and the Packers’ coaching staff have “got to find a way to get it done” regardless of who’s on the field. A few days after the Falcons loss, LaFleur directly criticized the offensive line’s fundamentals. “II think that’s where the majority of our focus will lie is in terms of our pass sets and how we’re passing off twists, how we punch,” he said. “All that stuff, it’s got to improve in a hurry.” That’s a particularly telling bit of criticism, because Butkus himself has identified improving fundamentals as one of the core aspects of his job. In 2025, Butkus was asked specifically what Jordan Morgan needed to improve to earn a full-time starting job, and Butkus responded that it was all about fundamentals — which he and the other coaches would work to help him improve. “So you’d better be good at technique, and that’s what we have to do constantly, be fanatics about working your technique and making sure if you’re letting defenders in your chest, you better be better with your hands,” Butkus said. “And that’s our job as coaches, help him with that.” Previous linemen have praised Butkus and offensive coordinator Adam Stenavich for helping them improve their fundamentals. The most pointed praise came from former Packers guard Jon Runyan. “Coach Steno, Coach Butkus, they make it so simple and it’s so easy to understand so that we go out there, we take everything they tell us from the film room onto the field and it’s just really easy to follow,” he said in 2021. “They just do a really good job of holding all of us to a really high standard and making sure that we know our stuff and they feel comfortable. They’re just doing their job at such a high level, it makes it a lot easier for us.” Why, then, are there repeated questions and concerns from the head coach about the offensive line’s fundamentals? It seems telling that the Runyan quote comes from 2021, when Adam Stenavich was a full-time offensive line coach and Butkus was merely his assistant. Both have been promoted since then; in 2022, Stenavich made the jump to offensive coordinator, while Butkus got the promotion to offensive line coach. Since then, it doesn’t seem like hyperbole to say the offensive line has been in a steady state of decline. Personnel plays a role in that; the Packers’ line is certainly less talented now than it was in the early Matt LaFleur era. But a coach’s job is to work with what he’s got, and many of the Packers’ early season struggles centered on Donovan Jennings and Jacob Monk, two players who had been in the Packers’ system for years. Both had several seasons of development under their belt, tutored all the while by Luke Butkus. If they weren’t ready to go when finally called upon, who’s to blame other than their position coach? The near-automatic response to LaFleur’s reticence to move on from struggling coaches is loyalty, but I’m not sure where that comes from in this particular instance. LaFleur and Stenavich go way back; Stenavich first worked with LaFleur as a practice squad member of the Houston Texans while LaFleur was a low-level assistant on Gary Kubiak’s staff. But there’s no such connection with Luke Butkus. He arrived courtesy of Nathaniel Hackett, with whom he’d worked for the Jacksonville Jaguars. His relationship with LaFleur began in 2019; it’s not like there’s some deep-seated relationship there. Maybe it’s just LaFleur’s general hesitance toward firing anyone rearing its head. Maybe there’s more going on behind the scenes than we’re seeing publicly. Maybe the second this season ends, Butkus will be out of a job. But for now, it seems like the man that should be getting rightly criticized — and in some cases, actually is facing some not-so-veiled criticism — is viewed as untouchable. In a season on the brink of total collapse, that’s hard to understand.

title: Green Bay Packers News: Do the Packers have any reason for hope?
summary: Predicting the end of the Packers’ season is about the easiest take you can make right now. The 2026 Packers seem like a solved problem. Their offensive line is so bad that opposing teams have no reason to respect the run game and little reason to fear the passing game if they can get pressure […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - NOVEMBER 15: Jordan Love #10 of the Green Bay Packers looks to pass against the Minnesota Vikings during the second quarter at Lambeau Field on November 15, 2026 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Michael Reaves/Getty Images) | Getty Images Predicting the end of the Packers’ season is about the easiest take you can make right now. The 2026 Packers seem like a solved problem. Their offensive line is so bad that opposing teams have no reason to respect the run game and little reason to fear the passing game if they can get pressure on Jordan Love, which, at this point, is about as easy as standing up and walking slowly forward as the Packers’ wholly inept offensive line flails their ineffective limbs in your general direction. That solved problem seems to indicate we know how the Packers will meet their demise. Either in the playoffs or, just as likely, before the postseason, the Packers will meet a team or series of teams that can exploit their incredibly obvious weakness and will beat them. They’ll either miss the playoffs or get bounced shortly after they begin. But what if that doesn’t happen? What if the Packers can hold off opposing teams just enough to give Jordan Love a chance to do what he needs to do? What if they actually can prove some resilience? What if they can get just healthy enough up front to put together an offensive line that keeps Love alive for a little while? That may not be entirely likely, but it’s not pie in the sky either. If they can get just good enough up front to make the line anything other than a total liability, maybe there’s a chance for this team yet. It’s not a huge chance, but if you’re looking for a reason for hope, it’s about all you’ve got. Otherwise we may just as well get the clock started on the offseason now. The NFL, in its infinite wisdom, has determined that it wants to claim the Wednesday before Thanksgiving as yet another special day for the league. Pro […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MASSACHUSETTS - NOVEMBER 8: Head Coach Matt LaFleur of the Green Bay Packers walks to the field prior to the game against the New England Patriots at Gillette Stadium on November 8, 2026 in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Kathryn Riley/Getty Images) | Getty Images For the first time in, well, maybe ever, the Green Bay Packers will have more rest between their next two games than they will get during their bye week. The NFL, in its infinite wisdom, has determined that it wants to claim the Wednesday before Thanksgiving as yet another special day for the league. Pro football’s schedule creep will never be over, not until the NFL finds a way to dominate every single day in the fall, and this is just the latest example. Unfortunately, the Packers (as well as the Los Angeles Rams) are the league’s guinea pigs for this next calendar expansion, with the two teams being set to play their Week 12 game next Wednesday night. Both teams have a bye in Week 11, ensuring that they do not have to play on a short week. That’s a good thing, right? Well, yes and no. It’s certainly untenable for NFL teams to play games with just two days of rest, which would have been the situation had the teams played a normal Sunday game in Week 11. Instead, with the Packers and Rams last playing on Sunday of Week 10 on November 15, they will have nine full days of rest before they face off on November 25. A Sunday-Wednesday sequence with an off week in between features 9 days of rest. That’s all well and good, but it’s the same as playing a Thursday Night Football game followed by a Sunday game the following week. Given the long grind of an 18-week NFL season, a few extra days of rest is certainly welcome. But having 9 days off between games is a significantly shorter break than the 13 days off that a team normally would get off for a full normal bye week. In fact, this sequence means that Packers actually get one more day of rest between their Weeks 12 and 13 games than they do between Week 10 and Week 12 with their “bye week” in between. Green Bay faces the New Orleans Saints on Sunday of Week 13, with that game taking place on December 6; that’s 10 full days of rest, effectively giving the Packers back-to-back mini-byes instead of a full week off. The Rams, meanwhile, have an even weirder setup. After 9 days of rest between Weeks 10 and 12, they have seven days off ahead of their Week 13 game, which is a Thursday Night Football matchup with the Kansas City Chiefs. (The Chiefs, for their part, are in the night game on Thanksgiving Day, putting them on normal rest.) The Rams then get their extra mini-bye after that Thursday game, as they play the San Francisco 49ers on Sunday afternoon in Week 14. Packers Rest Week 10-Week 12: 9 days Week 12-Week 13: 10 days Week 13-Week 14: 6 days (normal week) Rams Rest Week 10-Week 12: 9 days Week 12-Week 13: 7 days Week 13-Week 14: 9 days The Packers already had two mini-byes this season, having played a pair of Thursday Night Football games in the first half of the year. They did win both of the games that they played on extra rest — Week 4’s 17-14 victory over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers and the 45-27 demolition of the New England Patriots in Week 9. Even after this strange stretch, the Packers will still have yet another long mini-bye awaiting them towards the end of the season. Green Bay plays their rematch with the Bears on Christmas Day — a Friday — before hosting the Houston Texans the following week on Monday Night Football. That sequence sets up yet another 9-day rest situation, equivalent to a Thursday-Sunday layoff.

title: Stenavich on Packers’ starting offensive line vs. Rams: ‘I don’t know’
summary: Green Bay Packers offensive coordinator Adam Stenavich, formerly the team’s offensive line coach, was pretty blunt with his criticism of the team’s offensive line this week. “I don’t think anyone up front had a good performance,” he said of the unit’s effort on Sunday. Stanavich, in a press conference on Tuesday, added, “We had some […]
full_text: (Photo by Perry Knotts/Getty Images) | Getty Images Green Bay Packers offensive coordinator Adam Stenavich, formerly the team’s offensive line coach, was pretty blunt with his criticism of the team’s offensive line this week. “I don’t think anyone up front had a good performance,” he said of the unit’s effort on Sunday. Stanavich, in a press conference on Tuesday, added, “We had some pretty hard conversations yesterday.” The Packers’ staff met with players on Monday to “flush” the loss (in head coach Matt LaFleur’s words) before their players were given three off days as part of their split bye week . When asked about the team’s plan at guard, which has featured a rotating cast of characters week to week, Stenavich replied, “We got to evaluate what’s going on with everybody. I’m not going to tell you, one way or the other, because I don’t know.” He was later pressed on who the team’s best five were, if everyone was fully healthy. Stenavich responded, “I think we have a firm grasp on the best group, not necessarily the top five, but the top six, seven, and it’s all open to competition” So far, the Packers’ offensive line has played 13 players up front in 2026. Eight different line combinations have played at least 11 snaps together, while five of them have played at least 66 snaps together on offense. The most common line combination this year, so far, has been: Jordan Morgan, Laken Tomlinson, Sean Rhyan, Travis Glover and Anthony Belton. In total, that group has played 31 percent of the team’s offensive snaps, 189 total snaps. The only player who has been a full-time preferred starter to not miss action this year for the Packers’ line has been left tackle Jordan Morgan, easily the best player of the group in 2026. Injuries still loom, as there’s a question on whether or not Rhyan will be able to suit up, beyond just the question mark at guard — reps that have gone to Tomlinson, Glover, Aaron Banks and Kevin Zeitler this year. Stenavich wouldn’t discuss the Zeitler injury in the press conference, simply stating that Zeitler was “dinged up” in practice to the point where he couldn’t play on Sunday. He did confirm what LaFleur said this week: That the plan going into this week of prep was for Zeitler to start at right guard for the Packers. Glover ended up replacing Zeitler, instead of Banks — who is still on the injury report with two separate injuries. Banks was healthy enough to be active for the game, but he did not play a snap of offense. Even when the offense’s starters were benched in garbage time, the Packers’ starting line finished the game against the Vikings.

title: Groupthink: What to make of this Texans’ season?
summary: Texans fall to 3-6. What’s to make of the rest of this season? L4Blitzer: 8 games…only 8 games left. Mathematically, the team could still reach double-digit wins, but does anything about the 2026 Texans scream an 8-0/7-1 run to finish the regular season? Does anything scream 6-2 to get Ryans’ fourth straight winning season? Sure, […]
full_text: CLEVELAND, OHIO - NOVEMBER 15: Isaiah McGuire #57 and Myles Harden #26 of the Cleveland Browns sack C.J. Stroud #7 of the Houston Texans during the third quarter at Huntington Bank Field on November 15, 2026 in Cleveland, Ohio. (Photo by Nick Cammett/Getty Images) | Getty Images Texans fall to 3-6. What’s to make of the rest of this season? L4Blitzer: 8 games…only 8 games left. Mathematically, the team could still reach double-digit wins, but does anything about the 2026 Texans scream an 8-0/7-1 run to finish the regular season? Does anything scream 6-2 to get Ryans’ fourth straight winning season? Sure, the injuries hurt literally and figuratively, but the Texans could and should have won against Cleveland. Now…coaches will be working not to get ready for the postseason, but to either save their jobs or prep for the next ones. The players? They will play, but if they have nagging injuries, do they power through, or do they start making business decisions? I don’t see Houston losing out, but the way they are playing and coaching, a losing record seems all but certain. At least we aren’t the Chargers? That’s about it for positives right now. VBallRetired: Houston reeled off 12 straight wins last year so they are mathematically able to go 11-6. 9-8 or 8-9 feel much more likely. Neither of those results are enough to reach the playoffs, obviously. I place this loss clearly in Nick Caley’s lap and he seems to be a convenient scapegoat anyway. Cleveland made adjustments and he clearly didn’t. He was given two opportunities to put the game on ice and turtled instead. Much of the season though goes to the defense for key failures in key moments. This coaching staff needs more brain power and less buddy power. Ryans might need more help being creative on defense too. Patrick H.: The Texans have not officially been eliminated, but at this point Houston needs a planet-realignment-level of occurrence for it to happen. And does anyone see this team, this team that went up 17-0 against Cleveland only to lose after giving up 20 unanswered points, this team being able to pull off a planet-realignment? Because I sure don’t. I’ve tried to. I really have. But there is something standing in the way of this team being able to pull off such wonders on a regular basis. It’s coaching. We all know that Nick Caley is an empty headset and, if the Texans were clever, would leave him at the bus station in Cleveland and tell him to figure it out on his own. Maybe he makes it back, maybe he doesn’t, either way, he’s not your problem anymore. I cannot speak for anyone else, but after today, I will never allow myself to be tricked by Nick Caley’s offense again. It’s just a dead fish. But the Texans’ problems go beyond the offense that gives us all headaches. Houston plays sloppy, lacks discipline, and that lack of discipline has resulted in a lot of penalties per game over the course of DeMeco Ryans’ coaching career with the Texans. The offense has enough trouble putting points on the board without regularly shooting themselves in the foot with inexcusable false start and illegal formation penalties. The defense is apparently bad enough that they can’t afford idiotic “too many men on the field” penalties. The special teams are a shadow of what they once were with terrible punting, terrible returns, and penalties on every other appearance. It’s all slop. And all of that can be laid at the feet of coaching. I wanted DeMeco Ryans to be THE ANSWER. The one who would bring balance to the force, to steal another pop culture reference. He was the one who would bring the Lombardi to Kirby Drive. He was the one who would get us there with his staunch, unbreakable defense; the stuff we saw in San Francisco. It was going to be a wonder to behold. Where did that go? Where did the golden season go? It all went away because the current coaching order either can’t or won’t correct the underlying problems facing this team. This season isn’t mathematically over, but it’s over emotionally for a lot of Texans fans. That was the last gust of wind from the electric fan propelling the sail before shorting out and catching on fire. It’s going to be hard for anyone to bounce back from, again, being a chic Super Bowl pick to possibly having a top five draft pick. Heads. Must. Roll. The only question is whose and how many? Mike Bullock: Texans fans: Waiting for Next Season Since 2002 Vballretired nailed it: “more brain power, less buddy power”. Honestly, it seems like a bunch of friends, hanging out and getting paid to “play” football team. And, we all know that can’t be true – can it? These are professionals, making million$ to win football games, yet, the product on the field isn’t what thousands could buy, much less millions. Last season they wasted a great defense. This season they’re wasting a great C.J. Stroud. In the meantime, cue the empty seats or worse, seats filled with fans of the opposing team. Fire Caserio. Ryans. Caley, et al. Time to erase the white board and draw up a new team cause this one isn’t getting any closer than Bill O’Brien or Kubiak or Capers… The Texans are the only team in the past 50 seasons to lose 5 times within their 1st 9 games when tied or leading in the final 2 minutes — Doug Clawson (@doug_clawson) November 15, 2026 VBallRetired: Making history baby! Joe Critz: To me, the playoffs are almost certainly not happening this year, and that is a colossal disappointment considering the expectations entering the season. For the final half of this season, the Texans’ organization should pivot from the focus on winning and instead look inwards – at themselves, at the coordination and effectiveness of the coaching staff, and at all layers of the roster. It’s time for DeMeco Ryans and Nick Caserio to get introspective and determine, 1. what decisions were made that led them to this point; and 2. what steps need to be taken to be a better team and coaching unit in 2027. I completely agree with Scott that Nick Caley’s (or Cole Popovich or whoever on the offensive coaching staff) failure to adjust in the second half of the Browns game cost the team, and even though the Texans’ offense is at least statistically improved from last year, this is not the first time Caley has severely disappointed us. It’s time to challenge him and his staff – now that the season is basically over, the Texans coaching staff shouldn’t be afraid to get weird, experiment with play designs, and get rookies, backups, and young playmakers (like Febechi Nwaiwu, Brevin Jordan, or Marlin Klein) more involved. See what pieces of this roster are worth building upon for next season, what young players might become the building blocks of the next era of Texans football, and which ones won’t fit the bill. The same thing should apply for the defense, as well, as their collapse has been one of the most stunning developments of this NFL season, and major work will need to be done to exercise the demons that haunt them. The need for better depth at safety and linebacker is very apparent, so you might as well throw Jaylin Smith, Kamari Ramsey, and Wade Woodaz out there at random points throughout the season to see what they got cookin. Coverage, tackling, reaction time, and turnovers are all spots where the defense regressed from 2025, so it’s time to figure out what changes can be made to the starting lineup to get them back on track. But, this is where another layer to Houston’s failure this season rears its head. Kenneth has been very vocal in his disappointment with the 2026 draft class, and he has plenty of reason to be. Here was the moment for Nick Caserio to establish himself and his staff as one of the league’s premiere drafting organizations. They had clear objectives entering the 2026 offseason and draft, addressed them right off the bat with their first and second picks, and then…proceeded to have maybe the most disappointing draft in recent history. If Rutledge, McDonald, and Nwaiwu continue their upward…

title: Five Good Texans questions with Stampede Blue
summary: Chris Shepherd from Stampede Blue has been a good friend in the industry over the years and both of us had a huge challenge on our hands. We had two bad football teams going up against each other in prime time. That makes talking about these teams tough, but both of us have been here […]
full_text: Dec 28, 2025; Indianapolis, Indiana, USA; IIndianapolis Colts running back Jonathan Taylor (28) and cornerback Sauce Gardner (1) warm up before a game against the Jacksonville Jaguars at Lucas Oil Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Robert Goddin-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Chris Shepherd from Stampede Blue has been a good friend in the industry over the years and both of us had a huge challenge on our hands. We had two bad football teams going up against each other in prime time. That makes talking about these teams tough, but both of us have been here before and we are professionals, so we will make it work again. It is always a pleasure catching up with him. Our focus was more about the future of these two teams than what is going on right now on the field. Battle Red Blog: Both teams are having disappointing seasons so we both have questions to answer, but what is the big picture future for the Colts? Are there any good GM candidates? Do you think Steichen sticks around? Chris Shepherd: Big picture we’re looking at a full teardown. The Colts don’t have a good pass rushing edge defender, it’s high paid cornerbacks aren’t living up to their checks or the hype, they refuse to get their highly drafted and very good tight end involved in the passing game, their WR1 is unproven in that role (at least he’s an elite deep threat) and has barely played so far this season, they seem to be putting a lot of stock in a 27 (soon to be 28) year old running back who’s having a down year (for him), and most importantly they don’t have a quarterback who should be starting for an NFL team in 2026 or 2027, nor do they have a first round pick to try to find one. Short of a brilliant stroke of luck, something the Colts haven’t really had for more than a decade, good times seem to be several years away. There are a multitude of good GM candidates on paper. It’s tough to know from the outside who the real options will be but at this juncture my personal favorite is Catherine Hickman, assistant GM of the Cleveland Browns. Her resume is fairly short but she has excelled in every football job she has had as evidenced by her constant promotions. She seems to be a unique individual and the team that hires her may be getting a special GM. Also, I just want to watch Carlie Irsay-Gordon to hire the NFL’s first female GM just to watch the idiots react to it on Twitter. Shane has, I’d estimate, about a 40% chance of returning next year. Which is higher than any Colts fan would like but I do see a world where he’s allowed to return to eat up losses in a year that we should all expect to be pretty rough. BRB: Neither team is a realistic playoff team. What are you looking for for the remainder of the season? CS: Continued development from the team’s young players. As of today it seems that Chris Ballard’s final draft class with Indy might have been a good one. Offensively left guard Jalen Farmer has had moments, both very good and quite bad, with continued to play I hope to see more of the former. Running back Seth McGowan is eating into Jonathan Taylor’s carries and seems to have been an absolute steal in the seventh round. Linebackers CJ Allen and Bryce Boettcher have both looked good. Allen, quite good, Boettcher still has some things to figure out but he is an excellent athlete for the position. Safety AJ Halucy, has made a few splash plays here and there but hopefully with more time on the field his level of play will improve. BRB: Are you surprised Jonathan Taylor wasn’t dealt? Do you think Daniel Jones is still the QB in September of 2027? CS: Taylor? No. After Indy traded Quenton Nelson and DeForrest Buckner, and based on other comments made by ownership in the recent past, it seemed to me like Indy was willing to deal players on expiring contracts, guys who were unlikely to want to re-sign with the team. My belief was that they were setting up the next general manager with as much ammo as possible without making any decisions for players under contract in 2027, on their behalf. The next GM will come in on day one and instead of having to try to decide to who to keep and who to let walk for nothing and then negotiating contracts accordingly, they’ll have the ability to hit the ground running with a bevy of day two and three picks to try to stock the roster with as much young talent as possible. I don’t think DJ will be back, but stranger things have happened to the Colts in the last decade (Head Coach Jeff Saturday, comes to mind) so I wouldn’t rule it out. BRB: Looking towards March and April, what spots do you see the Colts targeting to get a quick turnaround? CS: The Colts haven’t had anyone record 10+ sacks in a season since Justin Houston in 2019, Indy has to use significant resources to solve their pass rushing issues if they want any hope of having any success before 2028. Beyond that, I see them investing in the draft at wide receiver as they’re currently starting three guys who might otherwise be on practice squads if not for Indy’s terrible receiving corps. Also, any time a new GM comes in, rosters experience massive turnover so it’s tough to predict at this juncture. BRB: FanDuel opened with the Texans being favored by ten. How do you see the game going? Are there any prop bets you feel comfortable recommending? CS: Ten points seems about right. We’re now two weeks beyond the trade deadline distractions and Indy played hard a week ago in Miami. I expect them to play hard and keep things relatively close (two scores is close for this team). Indy will try to run the ball with Taylor and McGowan and then dial up passes that Daniel Jones will look completely lost trying to throw. He’s good for at least one pick a game and if somehow he has the ball at the end of the game with a chance to drive down the field for a tie or a win, you can go ahead and bank on another interception. If Nico Collins’ receiving yardage over/under is sub 200 yards, you should definitely take the over. We want to thank Chris again for another great season of five questions. He is one of the more fun people in this industry to catch up with. The Colts are obviously in next year mode and the Texans are teetering on the verge of getting there. We will see if the action tonight throws them over the edge. We want to wish Chris and the Colts the best of luck for the remainder of the season. As per usual, we hope that luck begins on Friday morning.

title: Houston Texans vs. Indianapolis Colts: Injury Report
summary: The Houston Texans dropped yet another winnable game in Cleveland this past weekend. They came out firing, scoring 17 straight points, only to take their foot off the gas and allow the Browns to come back and eventually win the game on yet another game-winning drive. Houston’s defense has struggled to stop opposing offenses late […]
full_text: The Houston Texans dropped yet another winnable game in Cleveland this past weekend. They came out firing, scoring 17 straight points, only to take their foot off the gas and allow the Browns to come back and eventually win the game on yet another game-winning drive. Houston’s defense has struggled to stop opposing offenses late in games, which has been a major reason for most of their losses this season. The defense was without several key players, but that does not change the fact that this has been an ongoing issue throughout the year. The Texans now have an opportunity to get back in the win column against one of the worst teams in football, the Indianapolis Colts, who defeated Houston earlier this season. Here is a look at Wednesday’s injury report: DID NOT PARTICIPATE: -LB Azeez Al-Shaair (Groin/OUT) -TE Brevin Jordan (Foot/OUT) -RB Woody Marks (Concussion/OUT) -WR Marvin Harrison Jr. (Hamstring/OUT) -DE Danielle Hunter (Hamstring/OUT) FULL PARTICIPATION: -OT Blake Fisher (Thumb) -RG Reed Blankenship (Hand) -DB Jaylin Smith (Hamstring/QUESTIONABLE) -LB Jake Hummel (Groin) -OG Wyatt Teller (Back/QUESTIONABLE) -RB David Montgomery (Groin) -OG Keylan Rutledge (Neck/Shoulder) The good news is that Houston is getting running back David Montgomery back, who has not lived up to expectations this season outside of Week one. His presence is much needed, especially with the injury to Woody Marks. The previous matchup against Indianapolis did not go as planned, but if the Texans want any chance of making the playoffs, every game from here on out needs to be treated as a must-win.

title: Houston Texans NFL Power Rankings: Week 11
summary: “I’ve never seen anything quite like this. Never…it’s crazy.” – Conor Orr, Heed the Call Podcast ”…this was Eagles-esque.” – Steve Palazzolo, Check the Mic Podcast “CJ [Stroud] got blame, protection plan for blame, run game got blame, receivers got blame, [Nick] Caley got blame, [Cole] Popovich got blame…there is not a single person that […]
full_text: CLEVELAND, OH - NOVEMBER 15: Cleveland Browns defensive end Isaiah McGuire (57) and Cleveland Browns cornerback Myles Harden (26) sack Houston Texans quarterback C.J. Stroud (7) during the third quarter of the National Football League game between the Houston Texans and Cleveland Browns on November 15, 2026, at Huntington Bank Field in Cleveland, OH. (Photo by Frank Jansky/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images “I’ve never seen anything quite like this. Never…it’s crazy.” – Conor Orr, Heed the Call Podcast ”…this was Eagles-esque.” – Steve Palazzolo, Check the Mic Podcast “CJ [Stroud] got blame, protection plan for blame, run game got blame, receivers got blame, [Nick] Caley got blame, [Cole] Popovich got blame…there is not a single person that can watch that second half and think, ‘I did my job.’” – DJ Bien-Aime, Texans Cookout These are just some of the quotes from pundits, reporters, and analysts from around the league as they try to make sense of the Texans’ most recent, excruciating, 27-24 loss to the Cleveland Browns. If you had missed that game (or been wise enough to skip on watching), you may have thought that the world was crashing down on the Houston Texans Sunday afternoon, and that wouldn’t be far from the truth. This loss nearly guarantees Houston will not make the 2026 playoffs, pounding another nail into the coffin of one of their most ambitious seasons yet. Disappointment is something Texans fans have become accustomed to, but experiencing the air of hype surrounding this team deflate in just half of a season is a new low in the DeMeco Ryans era. In place of the hype, bitter feelings and debate about the team’s ability to make adjustments (or lack thereof) have filled the empty space. Texans guard Ed Ingram said he felt like there weren’t adjustments for the offense when it came to handling the pressure from Cleveland. pic.twitter.com/dWhevMAVOr — Cody Stoots (@Cody_Stoots) November 16, 2026 Asked Texans OC Nick Caley about the ongoing notion that they’re trying and why that even matters. The faith in the process despite results. Why he feels comfortable hanging his cap on his body of work. pic.twitter.com/6dffubsW0J — Landry Locker (@LandryLocker) November 16, 2026 As spectators of the team and hopeless bystanders to their games, our lack of agency in the performance of the Texans creates a sense of impending doom as the games go on and the losses pile up. As Battle Red Blog analyst Scott Barzilla stated in his Value of Things post this week, “It is like watching a car wreck in slow motion. You try to yell but nothing leaves your vocal cords. You just sit there in silence knowing what is going to happen.” That helpless feeling often manifests itself at first as casual frustration with the team and the coaching staff, then develops into resentment or ridicule as the season enters dire straits, and then finally, into pure exasperation as playoff hopes come crashing down. A failure this significant demands punishment – simple adjustments and a re-shuffling of game-day duties will no longer cut it for many in the Texans’ community; Now, with a 3-6 record, many are calling for firings. Some are even calling for the entire coaching staff to be dumped and for the Texans to just reset that entire section of their organization because of how unacceptable their current record is. How can you take a roster that went 12-5 and looked primed for a championship run just one year ago and drive them into the ground like this? More importantly, how are problems that have haunted this era of Texans football (penalties, hot-and-cold offense, poor offensive line) since 2023 still causing problems in 2026? The early successes of the Texans’ front office bought them time to address this issue, but stagnation year after year has now driven the community to a breaking point. Where do they go from here? It’s anyone’s guess, but chances are, we haven’t reached the lowest point of the season just yet. Regardless if shaking up the coaching staff in the middle of the season is the right decision to make, the fact this has become a popular refrain gives you an idea of how far Houston’s star has fallen in just two months. How far will that star fall in this week’s power rankings? Well, let’s find out: NFL.COM : 17. Houston Texans (3-6) (Last Week: 16) Well, just as the Texans’ unlikely turnaround from an 0-4 start was gaining steam, the Browns showed up to ruin it. Houston’s blown 17-point lead was a microcosm of what has plagued the team throughout this season, and while C.J. Stroud has enjoyed an excellent bounce-back campaign, his ineffectiveness for most of the second half Sunday was both disappointing and painfully familiar to Texans fans. This just might be what Houston is this year. – Nick Shook ESPN: 16. Houston Texans (3-6) Week 10 result: Lost to the Browns 27-24 Week 10 ranking: 17 Non-QB MVP at midseason: Edge Will Anderson Jr . Despite the Texans’ defense regressing drastically from last season, Anderson is currently at the top of DraftKings’ odds for Defensive Player of the Year (+120). He has 39 combined tackles (21 solo, 18 assists), 10.5 sacks, two forced fumbles and one fumble recovery. His sack total leads the league, and he’s tied for 12th among edge rushers with a 22.6% pass rush win rate. – DJ Bien-Aime SPORTS ILLUSTRATED: 20. Houston Texans (3–6) Last week’s ranking: No. 16 Last week’s result: lost to Browns, 27–24 This week: vs. Colts The Texans’ defense was a unit that preyed on its opponents by presenting pure simplicity at the line and then winning at every position. A year later, opponents like Todd Monken are looking at coverages from a year ago that are still being run and preying on that same simplicity. – Conor Orr BLEACHER REPORT: 22. Houston Texans (3-6) Last Week: 19 Week 10 Result: Lost at Cleveland 27-24 The Houston Texans’ season isn’t over just yet, but Sunday’s loss to the Cleveland Browns was a major blow. The Texans came out of their bye and delivered a convincing win in Week 9, albeit against the winless Chargers. Unfortunately, they were unable to build any momentum in Week 10. Instead, Houston blew an early 17-0 lead and slid further behind in the AFC South race. C.J. Stroud has played well enough to finally earn his second contract, but little else has gone well for the Texans this season. The defense continues to underwhelm, and running back Woody Marks (concussion) joined David Montgomery on the injured list on Sunday. At this point, the playoffs are an extreme long shot. – Kris Knox CBS SPORTS: 19. Texans (3-6) (Last Week; 19) The defense let them down in the loss to the Browns and now at 3-6 they have major problems in terms of the playoff race. They blew a 17-0 lead. – Pete Prisco USA TODAY: 23. Houston Texans (22): Elite defense? They’ve lost four games this season after surrendering a lead inside the final two minutes. – Nate Davis YAHOO! SPORTS: 18. Houston Texans (3-6, LW: 15) Sunday was the fifth time this season that the Texans have given up a drive in the final minutes of regulation or overtime to lose a game. Houston was supposed to be one of the best defenses in the NFL. The Texans were second in EPA per play allowed last season. This season they’re 20th, despite having mostly the same personnel and coaches. While defensive success can fluctuate from season to season more than offensive success, the Texans’ decline is perplexing. If Houston finished just two of those five games, it would be above .500. “We have to play better — run defense, have to tackle better,” head coach DeMeco Ryans said, via Texans Wire . – Frank Schwab THE ATHLETIC: 23. full_text: Feb 28, 2023; Indianapolis, IN, USA; Houston Texans general manager Nick Caserio during the NFL combine at the Indiana Convention Center. Mandatory Credit: Kirby Lee-USA TODAY Sports It seems that judging by the comments here and elsewhere that a number of fans have reached the point of no return on this team. We have also seen more than a few players express some frustration with how things have been going. Obviously, that does not mean there is a mutiny. That would be irresponsible reporting at this point and would spill us into hot take territory. However, when seasons like this go south there are inevitable questions about who gets assigned blame and what happens to them? I think we can all agree that Nick Caley and Cole Popovich’s days are numbered. Is it even completely their fault? Heck, the team has had four late fourth quarter leads in one possession games and seen the defense give up the score every single time. I’d certainly understand anyone willing to give a pass to Caley and the rest of the offensive coaching staff. However, after watching what we watched on Sunday and coupling that with the horrible effort against the New York Giants, it seems that Caley really hasn’t grasped what would make this team a consistent offensive threat. That leaves two people clearly in the crosshairs and it seems amazing that either of these two would be here. I hate to look at one football game as changing everything, but the Browns loss in particular shows all kinds of issues that at least need to be talked about if not acted on. I clearly try to look at things rationally and logically, so there are four possibilities here. We will go in the order of most to least likely. Both Nick Caserio and DeMeco Ryans stay I know this is the least popular option on the board, but it is the most likely option. What would the justification be? Essentially, this pairing has been together for four seasons and they have been successful in three of them. So, this would be a bet on the fact that everyone deserves a mulligan and that both would learn from their mistakes and right this ship in 2027. Let’s ignore for the time being that Caserio has been on the job longer than that and has two other failed head coaching hires. Most people would consider that just the necessary time it took to fix Bill O’Brien’s mess. The roster is still in good shape and the cap appears to be in good shape as well. Yes, he did trade away some draft capital to get Marvin Harrison Jr. We will have to get to that in a minute when we look at the other possibilities. So, in essence this group would be hiring their third offensive coordinator and third offensive staff. We could editorialize beyond that, but those facts alone probably speak for themselves. Ryans stays and Caserio goes If it comes down to who has the most juice in the building it would have to be Ryans. For one, he has been there only the four seasons where Caserio has the extra two seasons to his name. That comes with the extra baggage of those decisions made before Ryans, but it also means he has had six years to get things like the offensive line right and failed to do so. I am not predicting a power struggle here, but if one occurs Ryans also has the advantage of being a franchise icon. In a game of finger pointing it becomes a battle between the team having good enough talent and not executing because of coaching and the team simply not having enough talent. It would be interesting to see how such an argument would play out. You could make a case either way and I certainly would argue both ways, but in this scenario we are simply listing what is most likely to happen. Caserio stays and Ryans goes This would mean that Caserio wins the power struggle over whether it was the talent or the coaching that went south. I actually would almost put this is the last option because I just don’t see it going down this way. There are just too many head scratching moves to make anyone buy an argument that Caserio isn’t the most culpable. Moreover, some of these choices were criticized at the time. Why did you have to trade draft capital to move up for Keelan Rutledge? Wouldn’t he have been there with your pick? Why did you trade a second rounder for Marvin Harrison when others were traded at the deadline for far less? Why in the hell are you drafting Marlon Klein at all much less in the second round? Was anyone else really going to draft him before the fourth round? Why are we going with the same buy a bunch of cheap guys on the offensive line for the third season in a row? That strategy didn’t work the two times before. Wasn’t Reed Blankenship one of the worst safeties in football in 2025? I could keep going, but you get the idea. I’m just not buying Caserio having more juice than Ryans. Both of them get the boot I think this would be the vote of most of the more vocal fans. Here’s the main problem with it: the Texans have never done this in their 25 year history. They’ve never sacked both at the same time. The closest would be Dom Capers and Charlie Casserly, but even they were separated by a matter of months. The secondary problem is a problem of classic overreactions. If you fire a coach and general manager every time you have a bad season you are going to have a revolving door at both positions. For these reasons, I just don’t see this outcome as likely. I imagine a good percentage of the fanbase would choose that, but I also wonder how much that fluctuates depending on the results of the most recent game. The Cleveland game obviously points to major coaching issues and if that continues this option could become more likely. The end result is likely that there will be some better games mixed in and therefore the emotions won’t be so strong. What is my vote? Honestly, I have seen quite enough of the Nick Caserio experience to last a lifetime. A part of my calculus on this is the fact that this is the first major failure of the Ryans era. He has never seen his defenses struggle like this even going back to his San Francisco days. He has been hit in the mouth and it is time for him to respond. Sometimes that takes an offseason to engineer. Having been a coach before, I know how hard it is to adjust when you are right in the middle of it. Caserio has tried the same thing over and over again and gotten the same result. He has gone cheap on the line. He has hired buddies for the coaching staff. These things have not worked, but he keeps going back to that well. I don’t think it is a good idea to cut coaches free just because they failed once. I think Ryans deserves a chance to fix it, but firing Caserio clearly puts Ryans on notice. He must hire an experienced coordinator and not go the first time coordinator route yet again. This might be where ownership steps in and forces a coordinator on him. Of course, that is just my opinion, I am sure you have some of your own and this is your opportunity to share them.

title: Colts being 12.5-point underdogs to the 3-6 Texans says it all
summary: I keep asking myself if this is rock bottom for the Indianapolis Colts. The disastrous season when Peyton Manning went down was certainly rock bottom. The difference was, with the first overall pick, the franchise had a shovel to dig itself out. There is no shovel. No pick axe. Not even a lantern to lead […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - SEPTEMBER 27: Daniel Jones #17 of the Indianapolis Colts fumbles the ball while being tackled during the fourth quarter of the game against the Houston Texans at Lucas Oil Stadium on September 27, 2026 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Todd Rosenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images I keep asking myself if this is rock bottom for the Indianapolis Colts. The disastrous season when Peyton Manning went down was certainly rock bottom. The difference was, with the first overall pick, the franchise had a shovel to dig itself out. There is no shovel. No pick axe. Not even a lantern to lead the way. Being an almost two touchdown underdog to a 3-6 team might be the worst version of rock bottom. The Colts have taken some tremendous shellackings over the years. Those were generally singular moments, though. You have to go back to the beginning of the Indianapolis iteration of the Colts to find many examples of a team this bad. Even then, a debate could be had over who was in worse shape. Those teams had zero expectations. An almost two-decade run of success means there is no turning back. That’s what makes 2026 tough to swallow. The Texans are 3-6. Maybe that’s a tough 3-6, but this team has still lost six times already this year and is expected to whoop the Colts on Thursday Night Football. How did it get so bad? The eternal optimists are probably grinding their teeth right now, but what’s the worst part about next year: the fact the Colts have no direction at quarterback or the fact they won’t have a first-round pick to get one? Having a stockpile of draft picks is only good if the Colts hit. That remains to be seen. For now, they are two touchdown underdogs to the team currently with the ninth overall pick. Ouch . What’s the solution? No clue. Where do the Colts go from here? Not my job to figure out. Ideally, this is rock bottom. Ideally, there is nowhere to go but up. Ideally, the Colts hit on multiple draft picks and can get this thing going again. That’s what we all want, a winner. We want to watch good competitive football. It’s hard to do that when your favorite team is in such a deep hole, though. Nothing left to do but climb.

title: Stampede Blue Reacts Survey (Week 11): Can the Colts restore fan confidence?
summary: Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Colts fans and fans across the country. The Indianapolis Colts finally snapped their five-game losing streak Sunday, escaping with a narrow 24-22 victory over the Miami Dolphins to improve to 3-7 on the […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - NOVEMBER 15: Head Coach Shane Steichen of the Indianapolis Colts looks on against the Miami Dolphins during an NFL football game at Lucas Oil Stadium on November 15, 2026 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Colts fans and fans across the country. The Indianapolis Colts finally snapped their five-game losing streak Sunday, escaping with a narrow 24-22 victory over the Miami Dolphins to improve to 3-7 on the season. While ending the losing streak was certainly a welcome development, the performance itself did little to suggest that Indianapolis has turned a corner. The Colts nearly squandered a 21-7 third-quarter lead against a struggling Dolphins team, benefiting from two missed field goals and a failed two-point conversion to secure the victory. With another difficult divisional matchup against the Houston Texans approaching Thursday night, there are still plenty of questions surrounding the team’s ability to compete consistently. Perhaps the biggest concern remains the offense, particularly quarterback Daniel Jones and head coach Shane Steichen’s continued commitment to him. Jones completed just 11 of 22 passes for 108 yards, one touchdown and two interceptions against Miami, while Jonathan Taylor and Seth McGowan combined for 160 rushing yards on only 28 carries. Tyler Warren, meanwhile, finished with just two receptions for one yard, despite being one of the team’s most talented receiving options. With the Colts having traded several established offensive players before the deadline, Steichen faces increasing pressure to adjust his game plan and make better use of the talent still available. Continuing to rely on an ineffective passing attack while the team’s most productive players receive limited opportunities is hardly a formula for sustained success. Last week’s Reacts survey revealed that only 17 percent of Colts fans believed the franchise was headed in the right direction, continuing a steady decline from 47 percent just three weeks earlier. The recent trades, disappointing performances and uncertainty surrounding the coaching staff and quarterback position have understandably left much of the fan base frustrated. However, the emergence of several younger players, combined with the organization’s efforts to accumulate draft capital, could provide some hope for the future. With the Colts now preparing for a divisional matchup against Houston and a new general manager expected to take over during the offseason, the question is whether Sunday’s victory has restored any confidence or whether fans remain convinced that Indianapolis is still years away from returning to contention. title: Colts’ Week 10 QB Analysis: Winning Ugly
summary: Thanks to the nflFastR project, Pro Football Focus for the timely sources of data. For those of you new to this, I will publish key QB stats each week judging how well the Colts’ QB performed. Yes, O-Line, receivers, and play-calling impact these numbers but they are primarily QB measures. I will probably modify the charts throughout the season. […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - NOVEMBER 15: Chop Robinson #44 of the Miami Dolphins reacts after Daniel Jones #17 of the Indianapolis Colts fumbles the ball at Lucas Oil Stadium on November 15, 2026 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Justin Casterline/Getty Images) | Getty Images Thanks to the nflFastR project, Pro Football Focus for the timely sources of data. For those of you new to this, I will publish key QB stats each week judging how well the Colts’ QB performed. Yes, O-Line, receivers, and play-calling impact these numbers but they are primarily QB measures. I will probably modify the charts throughout the season. Commentary will be brief but feel free to let me know in the comments that stats aren’t everything. (click charts for larger view) Daniel Jones has had plenty of bad games in his career, but this one might have been his worst. He couldn’t complete passes, he turned the ball over, and of the nine drives that didn’t end in an interception, six were three-and-outs that earned a total of 8 yards. But hey, at least he found the end zone once . . . ONCE! If it weren’t for a Colts defensive score and Miami missing two field goals, there’s no way we would have won this game. HOW WELL? mouseover definitions: arsr , edp , sg% , oz% , pr% , tip , ttt , adot , ay/c , yac , yacoe , yd/c , ac% , cpoe , aypa , drp , scr% , ta% , sck% , aa% , ny/d , ny/p , 1st% , td% , to% , qbsr , epa/p , adj/p The running game wasn’t great but the Colts relied on it much more heavily than the pass on early downs. (20th ARSR; 30th EDP) Jones faced a below average amount of pressure, with fairly normal timing both before pressure arrived and when he released the ball. So, he wasn’t rushed. (20th PR%; 16th TIP; 17th TTT) Despite that though, Jones threw mostly short passes, and his completions generated very little yardage through the air. Yards after the catch were roughly average, but that wasn’t nearly enough to compensate for the lack of air yards, leaving him near the bottom of the league — YET AGAIN!— in total yards per completion. (28th ADOT; 28th AY/C; 14th YAC; 15th YCOE; 26th YD/C) Jones completed just 11 of 22 passes, falling dramatically short of expectations. Combined with the limited yardage on those completions, that left him dead last in the league in adjusted yards per attempt. (31st AC%; 32nd CPOE; 32nd AYPA) Jones scrambled twice, threw the ball away once and took only 1 sack, leaving his overall abandoned-attempt rate near league average. (12th DRP; 9th SCR%; 13th TA%; 21st SCK%; 17th AA%) Even with relatively few abandoned attempts, the passing game generated very little yardage, leaving Jones near the bottom of the league — YET AGAIN!— in net yards per dropback and quarterback play. (26th NY/D; 27th NY/P) Jones struggled to move the chains, generating just five passing first downs and throwing only one touchdown. (29th 1ST%; 17th TD%) Turnovers were a big problem as he threw two interceptions, including a disastrous pick-six, giving him one of the highest turnover rates of the week. (4th TO%) Overall, Jones was awful at consistently generating positive plays, producing positive EPA on just 8 of 26 quarterback plays. His few successful plays were completely overwhelmed by the negatives, particularly the pick-six, leaving him with an atrocious -0.65 EPA per play, the second-worst performance in the league this week. (30th QBSR; 31st EPA/P) mouseover definitions: ay< , dp% , ay/c , yac , yd/c , ac% , aypa , drp% , aypa , ta% , ypa , sck% , ny/a , scr% , ny/d , car% , ny/p , 1st% , any/p , td% , any/p , to% , any/p , epa/p , opd , adj/p Jones’ efficiency curve fell sharply right from the start, with no deep completions and very little yardage through the air. Yards after the catch provided the only significant boost, but his abysmal completion rate wiped out that improvement, leaving him dead last in adjusted yards per attempt. The two interceptions, including the disastrous pick-six, dragged his efficiency towards the bottom, leaving him with an atrocious -0.65 EPA per play, ranking 31st in the league. Jones produced positive EPA on just 8 of 26 quarterback plays (30.8%), with most of his performance dominated by negative plays. A brief second-quarter surge, highlighted by a 30-yard completion (+2.8 EPA) and his lone touchdown (+2.2 EPA), provided some much-needed positive value. Unfortunately, that was overwhelmed by two interceptions, particularly the disastrous third-quarter pick-six that cost the Colts a staggering 10.1 EPA. He then failed to produce a single positive play in the fourth quarter. Even without the pick-six, Jones would have finished with negative EPA, but that one catastrophic play helped drag his final efficiency down to an abysmal -0.65 EPA per play. You guys can read graphs, right? Down is bad. HOW FAR? Jones opened with three straight incompletions, including two deep shots, before briefly finding a rhythm with a string of short completions, but interceptions repeatedly disrupted any momentum. After the pick-six, his six remaining throws gained just 21 yards combined. Jones reverted to shorter throws, with his average target depth falling from 8.2 to 6.6 yards. His completed passes averaged just 3.9 yards downfield, continuing a bad trend of increasingly shallow completions. As I have said many times, throwing short is not necessarily a bad thing as long as you make a lot of completions and get a lot of YAC. Mahomes throws shorter than Jones, but he gets a lot of yards out of it, while Jones does not. TO WHO? Wow, look at that fierce competition to try to get to a whole 30 yards! Josh Downs continues to lead the Colts in receiving yards even though he isn’t on the team. That’s something. Treadwell’s TD put him into the short-depth-high-value area of the chart. Dulin’s one completion was impressive. Everyone else, please stay after class. Lot’s of blue dots below the green line. Not good. HOW ACCURATE? Jones had his worst completion rate and CPOE of the season — and I am guessing as a Colt, but I am too lazy to look it up. HOW FAST? This is literally the only graph on this page, where I can say something even remotely positive — he didn’t hold on to the ball too long. TO WHERE? Red bad. I can’t even.

title: Colts CB Justin Walley earns AFC Defensive Player of the Week honors after momentous strip-sack
summary: On the opening snap of the second half against the Miami Dolphins, Indianapolis Colts cornerback Justin Walley disguised a nickel blitz to come screaming off the edge against an empty pocket. Dolphins quarterback Kyle McCord tried to escape, but Walley closed in to lay a hit before McCord had enough time to react. Walley punched […]
full_text: On the opening snap of the second half against the Miami Dolphins, Indianapolis Colts cornerback Justin Walley disguised a nickel blitz to come screaming off the edge against an empty pocket. Dolphins quarterback Kyle McCord tried to escape, but Walley closed in to lay a hit before McCord had enough time to react. Walley punched the football out of his grasp for a strip-sack and sent the leather tumbling into the end zone. Defensive tackle Adetomiwa Adebawore hustled to recover the fumble for a touchdown, giving Indianapolis a defensive score that ultimately proved to be the winning play in its 24-22 victory over Miami inside Lucas Oil Stadium. Walley admitted as soon as defensive coordinator Lou Anarumo dialed up the playcall, he knew it was his moment to wreak havoc in the backfield and terminate Miami’s drive just seconds after it got started. Walley 🌎 pic.twitter.com/7yonWEY9jJ — Indianapolis Colts (@Colts) November 18, 2026 The momentum-shifting play earned Walley AFC Defensive Player of the Week honors, the first league-wide recognition of his NFL career. Walley finished with five tackles, including two tackles for loss, two pass deflections and a pivotal strip-sack. His standout performance makes him the first defensive back to reach that statline in a single NFL game since at least 1993. AFC Players of the Week! (Week 10) @JoeyB | @JustinWalley_ | @cameronglittle pic.twitter.com/MHj5lU4pHP — NFL (@NFL) November 18, 2026 Indianapolis managed to score just three points from its offense in the second half, letting a comfortable two-possession advantage shrink to two points as Miami mounted a rally. Walley’s strip-sack gave the Colts enough cushion to withstand the Dolphins’ late push. The 24-year-old posted a 91.2 Pro Football Focus defensive grade in Week 10, which was the highest among all cornerbacks and third-best among all NFL players. He made life difficult for McCord in his first NFL start, giving up just three catches on six targets for a measly 13 yards. Through 10 games, Walley has collected 40 tackles, including three tackles for loss, two sacks, three forced fumbles, and five pass deflections. His 22 defensive stops rank second among all NFL cornerbacks this season. Great play by Justin Walley. The team was right about this kid. #Colts #ForTheShoe #Dolphins #MIAvsIND pic.twitter.com/UqpALva7EE — Chris Shepherd (@NFLscheme) November 15, 2026 The Colts selected Walley in the third round with the 80th overall pick in the 2025 NFL Draft out of Minnesota, with intentions to add a young, versatile nickel to their secondary. His NFL introduction didn’t go according to plan, because Walley missed his entire rookie season after suffering a torn ACL during a joint-practice with the Baltimore Ravens in training camp, delaying an early opportunity to establish himself on the field. For a player who missed his rookie campaign, the recognition represents the journey it took to return to the gridiron. Walley is the fourth Colts cornerback to earn AFC Defensive Player of the Week honors over the past decade, joining Kenny Moore II (twice), Jaylon Jones and Xavier Rhodes. The Colts (3-7) needed someone on the defensive side of the ball to make a play and halt the Dolphins’ first drive of the second half. Adebawore deserves credit for recovering the football, but Walley’s fingerprints knocked the football loose into the blue turf for the fumble recovery touchdown.

title: 5 Questions with Big Blue View: Are John Harbaugh’s Giants Legit?
summary: As the Jacksonville Jaguars prepare to face the New York Giants in Week 11, we exchanged questions with Ed Valentine of Big Blue View to learn more about the opposing side. Question 1: Do you have any reservations about John Harbaugh, or are you all in on Big Blue’s new coach? I don’t have any […]
full_text: EAST RUTHERFORD, NEW JERSEY - SEPTEMBER 13: head Coach John Harbaugh of the New York Giants reacts during the game against the Dallas Cowboys at MetLife Stadium on September 13, 2026 in East Rutherford, New Jersey. (Photo by Evan Bernstein/Getty Images) | Getty Images As the Jacksonville Jaguars prepare to face the New York Giants in Week 11, we exchanged questions with Ed Valentine of Big Blue View to learn more about the opposing side. Question 1: Do you have any reservations about John Harbaugh, or are you all in on Big Blue’s new coach? I don’t have any reservations. Harbaugh has completely changed the expectations for the franchise, and has brought credibility. Is he perfect? No. You can poke a lot of holes in the way the loss to the Commanders unfolded last Thursday. But, Harbaugh has raised the floor. He is exactly what the franchise needed. Question 2: Between J.J. McCarthy, Malik Nabers, and Cam Skattebo, who is the focal point of the Giants’ offense? Well, “focal point’ is an interesting way to put it. The offense was built for Jaxson Dart, not J.J. McCarthy. Bringing in McCarthy simply allows them to run the offense closer to the way they intended to. The passing attack is built around Nabers and Isaiah Likely. The Giants have tried since the spring to find a better RB1 than Skattebo, but he is what they have. Question 3: If you were game planning against the Giants’ defense, which weaknesses would you attack? First of all, I would say know where No. 52 (Arvell Reese) is at all times, and have an idea of what he is going to do. I would say you want to probe the Giants with the run. They are good there, until they aren’t. They have been prone to giving up the big play on the ground. The Giants will blitz Trevor Lawrence a lot. Fewer ads Seamlessly jump between communities and conversations Faster commenting and posting experience! Download the SB Nation app on iOS or Android . Question 4: Who are some under-the-radar players that Jaguars fans should know of before Sunday’s kickoff? Neither of the answers I am going to give are really under-the-radar guys, but they are important players for New York. On offense, tight end Isaiah Likely has been everything the Giants hoped for and more when they signed him. He already has career highs in catches and receiving yards. On defense, former first-round pick Deonte Banks and former Jaguar Greg Newsome have been outstanding. Defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson is letting them press and cover man-to-man a lot, which is exactly what both do well. Question 5: Do you expect the Giants to cover as 6.5-point underdogs, and do you have a favorite player prop for the game? Of their nine games, eight have been decided by one score. Their 36-24 victory over Arizona was a six-point game until the last play, when Banks returned an interception 98 yards to secure the victory. Out of the four wins, three of them were in Jacksonville, so let’s revisit all of the wins while hoping the Jags bring home another […]
full_text: JACKSONVILLE, FL - NOVEMBER 20: Wide receiver Plaxico Burress #17 of the New York Giants watches as linebacker Clint Ingram #51 of the Jacksonville Jaguars intercepts a pass intended for Burress at Alltel Stadium on November 20, 2006 in Jacksonville, Florida. The Jaquars defeated the Giants 26-10. (Photo by Doug Benc/Getty Images) | Getty Images Happy Giants Week, Big Cat County! This is a rare event, as the Jaguars have played the Giants only eight times in franchise history, and the series is currently tied. Out of the four wins, three of them were in Jacksonville, so let’s revisit all of the wins while hoping the Jags bring home another one on the road. The 1990s Week 2 at Alltel Stadium on September 7, 1997 Final score: Giants 13 – Jaguars 40 Attendance: 70,581 James Stewart and Natrone Means both scored two touchdowns. Steve Matthews threw for 252 yards and was sacked once. Means led the team with 85 rushing yards, and Jimmy Smith led with 117 receiving yards. Mike Hollis made the four attempted field goals. Travis Davis had a 23-yard interception. Clyde Simmons and Joel Smeenge recorded sacks. The 2000s Week 11 at Alltel Stadium on November 20, 2006 Final score: Giants 10 – Jaguars 26 Attendance: 67,164 A dominant Week 11 win with a 40:19 time of possession. David Garrard completed 19 out of 32 attempted passes for 249 yards. Fred Taylor and Maurice Jones-Drew scored touchdowns. Taylor led the team with 79 rushing yards, and Ernest Wilford led with 72 receiving yards. Josh Scobee made four field goals, the longest being from 48 yards. Deon Grant and Clint Ingram intercepted two passes from Eli Manning, and Bobby McCray sacked Manning for a loss of eight yards. The 2010s Week 13 at EverBank Stadium on November 30, 2014 Final score: Giants 24 – Jaguars 25 Attendance: 64,687 The Jags overcame a 21-point deficit, starting with Josh Scobee making a field goal to end the half. The defense stepped up to the plate with J.T. Thomas and Aaron Colvin returning fumbles for touchdowns. Marqise Lee led the team with 75 receiving yards, scored the only offensive touchdown, and the two two-point conversions failed. Blake Bortles completed 21 out of 35 attempted passes for 194 yards, was sacked seven times for a loss of 54 yards, and led the team with 68 rushing yards. Scobee made both attempted field goals. Geno Hayes, Sen’Derrick Marks, and Tyson Alualu sacked Eli Manning four times for a loss of 34 yards. Week 1 at MetLife Stadium on September 9, 2018 Final score: Jaguars 20 – Giants 15 Attendance: 77,992 T.J. Yeldon scored the offensive touchdown. Bortles completed 18 out of 33 attempted passes for 176 yards and was sacked once for a loss of eight yards. Yeldon led the team with 51 rushing yards, and Keelan Cole led with 54 receiving yards.
