title: Kellen Moore has run out of excuses in New Orleans
summary: How many more embarrassing losses do the New Orleans Saints have to suffer before it’s time to move on from Kellen Moore? Sunday’s 20-17 loss to the Carolina Panthers at the Caesars Superdome should have been the final straw. This was a game the Saints had every opportunity to win. Carolina committed an incredible 17 […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LA - NOVEMBER 15: Kellen Moore head coach of the New Orleans Saints looks on during the first half of a game against the Carolina Panthers at Caesars Superdome on November 15, 2026, in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Derick Hingle/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images How many more embarrassing losses do the New Orleans Saints have to suffer before it’s time to move on from Kellen Moore? Sunday’s 20-17 loss to the Carolina Panthers at the Caesars Superdome should have been the final straw. This was a game the Saints had every opportunity to win. Carolina committed an incredible 17 penalties for 152 yards, compared to just three penalties for 46 yards by New Orleans. The Panthers repeatedly shot themselves in the foot, yet the Saints couldn’t take advantage of the opportunities in front of them. Instead, New Orleans dropped to 3-6 and watched Carolina take sole possession of first place in the NFC South. The Saints managed just 222 total yards, couldn’t establish a running game even with Travis Etienne Jr. back and scored zero points in the first half. The running backs combined for just 24 yards on 17 carries, leaving Tyler Shough to shoulder far too much of the offensive responsibility. At some point, the excuses have to stop. Injuries, personnel issues and growing pains can only explain so much. Moore is in his second season, and the same problems that plagued this team last year continue to show up every Sunday. And now, it’s starting to regress his promising young quarterback. The Saints have struggled with preparation, offensive consistency, overall execution and closing out games during Moore’s tenure. Those are the habits of a poorly coached football team, and Moore has repeatedly failed to find answers. New Orleans needs a change. Sunday’s loss was another reminder that this current regime just isn’t getting the job done. The Saints cannot keep wasting opportunities in a division that remains wide open. It’s time for the Saints to stop pretending things are going to get better without making a change.

title: Travis Etienne Jr. looks to find his footing against Bears
summary: Travis Etienne Jr. returned to action for the New Orleans Saints this past weekend, but his first game back did little to change the team’s run game issues. After missing five games with a hamstring injury, Etienne finished the 20-17 loss to the Carolina Panthers with eight carries for 14 yards and three receptions for […]
full_text: DETROIT, MI - SEPTEMBER 13: New Orleans Saints running back Travis Etienne Jr. (3) cuts back to gain more yardage and a first down during the Detroit Lions versus New Orleans Saints game on Sunday September 13, 2026 at Ford Field in Detroit, MI. (Photo by Steven King/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Travis Etienne Jr. returned to action for the New Orleans Saints this past weekend, but his first game back did little to change the team’s run game issues. After missing five games with a hamstring injury, Etienne finished the 20-17 loss to the Carolina Panthers with eight carries for 14 yards and three receptions for 20 yards. It was a quiet afternoon for the running back, who had been expected to provide a boost to an offense that desperately needs more production from its backfield. The Saints couldn’t get much going offensively, and Etienne averaged just 1.8 yards per carry in his return. Still, there is reason to believe he can become a more productive part of the offense as he gets further removed from the injury. Before going on injured reserve, Etienne had rushed for 128 yards on 30 carries through his first three games with New Orleans. He also added 11 receptions for 51 yards. His ability to contribute as both a runner and receiver gives the offense another dynamic playmaker, but the Saints have to get him into a rhythm. The Saints will need more from that group when they travel to face the Chicago Bears next week. Etienne should have a better opportunity to settle into his role after getting his return to game action out of the way, although the workload and production will certainly need to improve. His return alone was not enough to fix New Orleans’ rushing attack against Carolina. The Saints need the version of Etienne they expected when he invested in him this offseason. A stronger performance against Chicago would be an important step toward giving the offense a more dependable run game and making his return meaningful.

full_text: The 5-3-1 New York Giants host the red-hot 7-2 Jacksonville Jaguars on Sunday. The game was flexed to a 4:25 EST window, and the Jaguars are currently favored by 6 points with a 46.5-point Over/Under. The Jaguars finish their three-game road trip in New York; they’ve beaten the Colts, Ravens, and Titans, scoring 115 points while allowing 40 over their last three games. Jacksonville is a true test for the Giants, who lost at home in a disappointing Thursday Night Football matchup to the Washington Commanders, 24-21. Offensive statistics Liam Coen’s Jaguars rank fourth in points per game, averaging 29.9. Only the Bills, 49ers, and Bengals score more points per game than the Jacksonville Jaguars. They’re 9th in total yards per game, with a 358.9-yard average, 241.1 passing yards per game (10th in the NFL), and 117.8 rushing yards per game (12th in the NFL). The Jaguars have rested starters in the fourth quarter in multiple contests this season. Jacksonville has a 46.8% third-down conversion rate, third in the NFL, and a 65.2% red-zone touchdown rate, fifth in the NFL. The Jaguars are an efficient offense with explosive weapons and a well-designed rushing attack led by second-year running back Bhayshul Tuten, who has 609 rushing yards ( 4.1 YPC ) and five touchdowns. Wide receiver Parker Washington is breaking out in his third season. He has caught 36 of 64 targets for 654 yards wtih six receiving touchdowns from Trevor Lawrence, who is having an excellent second season under Coen. Lawrence has completed 66% of his passes for 2,284 yards with 21 passing touchdowns and five interceptions. He’s been sacked 14 times and has 106 rushing yards. Jacksonville’s personnel The Jacksonville Jaguars lean on Tuten but do keep a mild rotation behind the budding star running back. Chris Rodriguez Jr. was brought in to be the hammer near the goal line. He maintains a role on the offense when the game is neutral and is the back in clean-up duty as well. He has 233 yards ( 3.9 YPC ) and four touchdowns this season. Ameer Abdullah is a change-of-pace back who still provides explosive upside, but did not play an offensive snap in Week 10. LeQuint Allen Jr. is a backup third-down back who sees 10-15% of snaps a game. Jacksonville has a deep rotation at wide receiver. Washington is the star emerging into his own, but long-time veteran Jakobi Meyers leads the team in snap share. He has caught 29 of 43 passes for 408 yards with two scores. Brian Thomas Jr. plays just less than half of the snaps, and he competes with rookie Josh Cameron for snaps; the latter sees some snaps in 12 personnel due to his blocking, and he caught a touchdown in Week 10. Brian Thomas Jr. looked to be an elite weapon after his stellar rookie season, but the former LSU product has been relegated to a situational role, and he was heavily rumored to be traded at the deadline, but he remains a Jaguar. He has caught 12 of 25 passes for 146 yards with two touchdowns. He’ll be on the field in 11 personnel. The Jaguars did an excellent job identifying Josh Cameron as an asset for them in the sixth round of the draft. The former Baylor product has caught 12 of 17 passes for 190 yards with three touchdowns. Travis Hunter is a full-time — and difference-making — cornerback for Jacksonville, but he still plays in certain offensive packages. He played just 8% of snaps on Sunday; he hasn’t eclipsed 13% of snaps on offense this season. The Jaguars have invested in their tight end room. Brenton Strange is their starter and plays over 70% of snaps. He has secured 32 of 40 targets for 365 yards with two touchdowns, including one last week against Tennessee. Jacksonville spent a second-round pick on Nate Boerkircher, and he provides solid blocking; he has caught 10 of 14 targets for 156 yards wtih two touchdowns. Quintin Morris and Tanner Koziol are the third and fourth tight ends on the roster. Starting left tackle Anton Harrison is on IR, and Walker Little has stepped into the lineup. Little has played excellent football in lieu of Harrison. Penei Sewell OT grades/ranks this season Run block 94.0/1st Pass block 85.5/3rd Absolute DOMINANCE pic.twitter.com/Lx0qoU3Xek — PFF (@PFF) November 17, 2026 Rookie Emmanuel Pregnon is playing good football in the run and pass game; he’s their starting left guard. Robert Hainsey is solid at center, but is out with an injury, and Ezra Cleveland is solid at right guard. Cole Van Lanen is the starting right tackle. The matchup Jacksonville is a problem. I expect Dennard Wilson to lean on the blitz and other creative ways to generate pressure, as he has almost all season. Jayden Daniels burnt the Giants for three third-down touchdowns when the Giants blitzed; Washington accounted for the Cover-0 approach well after New York effectively employed the approach in their Week 5 tie. Nevertheless, the Giants may attempt to bring extra pressure on Lawrence. According to SumerSports, up until Week 7, Trevor Lawrence was the QB most affected by pressure: Trevor Lawrence is the quarterback most affected by pressure pic.twitter.com/ZaYE4Kq83N — SūmerSports (@SumerSports) November 3, 2026 Jacksonville’s last three opponents—the Colts, Ravens, and Titans—did not apply much pressure to Lawrence, but the former Clemson Tiger improved when he faced pressure. This season, Lawrence has been above-average overall against the blitz, though. Per NFLNextGen, and Travis Holmes on X, here are Lawrence’s numbers against the Blitz: Yards p/att: 10th (1st) Passer Rating: 14th (1st) EPA: 3rd (4th) EPA per dropback: 2nd (4th) Comp %: 21st (6th) CPOE: 8th (8th) Air Yards per/att: 2nd (9th) Tight Window Throw %: 2nd (28th) Holmes summarizes it well here: Lawrence Passer Rating vs the blitz by week: 1) 89.6 vs Browns 2) 57.5 vs Broncos 3) 53.2 vs Patriots 4) 110.7 vs Bengals 5) 72.9 vs Eagles 6) 111.4 vs Texans 8) 93.8 vs Colts 9) 128.6 vs Ravens 10) 145.3 vs Titans Russian roulette if you blitz. ℍ𝕠𝕝𝕞𝕖𝕤 (@TravisDHolmes) November 17, 2026 Lawrence’s ability to burn a defense that sends extra rushers is undeniable, but not sending extra rushers is a PRECARIOUS situation for the opponents of Jacksonville. The Giants can rely on deception to manipulate and waste blockers to facilitate mismatches and/or free rushers into the pocket if they don’t blitz. Lawrence EPA per dropback from a clean pocket ranks first in the NFL. The Giant problem that arises if New York sticks to heavy pressure is Lawrence’s ability to quickly find a solution, like Washington did in Week 10. New York must be sound in tackling and avoid dumb penalties — playing efficient and disciplined football is the key to victory against a talented team like the Jaguars. Jacksonville shouldn’t struggle to run as Washington did, so New York must stay gap-disciplined; both Micah McFadden and Arvell Reese have done well in this regard over the last two weeks. If Lawrence quickly finds solutions early against pressure, Wilson should look to bail into coverage/contain looks on some third downs, focusing on slot-threat Parker Washington, who will have an advantage against Dru Phillips. It was years ago, but Wink Martindale defeated Jacksonville for the Giants in 2022 by dropping eight often-out-of-pressure looks; this could be a wise curveball for Wilson to use. title: Cam Skattebo will retire his backflip celebration
summary: New York Giants running back Cam Skattebo has a reputation as a wild man. He loves contact so much he routinely headbutted walls before games at Arizona state. Giants fans love seeing their resident caveman score touchdowns, but they won’t see any more of his trademark backflips this year. At least in the regular season […]
full_text: New York Giants running back Cam Skattebo does a back flip after scoring a touchdown. | Getty Images New York Giants running back Cam Skattebo has a reputation as a wild man. He loves contact so much he routinely headbutted walls before games at Arizona state. Giants fans love seeing their resident caveman score touchdowns, but they won’t see any more of his trademark backflips this year. At least in the regular season after the injury suffered by Detroit Lions edge defender Aidan Hutchinson. Hutchinson celebrated a sack by jumping in the air with a bit of forward velocity, tearing his ACL as he landed. This isn’t the first time this has happened to an edge defender after a sack. Fellow Lion’s defender Stephen Tulloch tore his ACL after sacking Aaron Rodgers with a similar celebration in September 2014, as did Bears defender Lamarr Houston a few weeks later . But 2014 is ancient history. This is now , and it’s enough to scare Skattebo off the flips. “It’s hard to see,” Skattebo told reporters after Wednesday’s practice. “I’m saying yeah (no more). Mentally, I’m like, ‘I’m not doing that.’ That ain’t going to happen to me.” “It’s [the standing backflip] actually kinda basic for people that start young,” a former D-1 gymanst told me. “There are kids in their single digits that can do a standing back flip.” “If you know what you’re doing it’s not risky,” they said. “But with age and weight, and just being tired from running up and down the field it can be more dangerous. If you open early you leave yourself at risk to landing short which would lead to a sprained ankle or twisted ankle. The worst case scenario is a broken ankle. If you land locked leg, that can cause a knee injury.” The risk, they said, really depends on the surface. “We have a spring mat or a trampoline, so the take off and landing isn’t bad. I personally wouldn’t do one on turf. But if I did a back flip on turf I would run into it. If you’re landing in the wrong position it may hurt.” This isn’t the first time concerns have cropped up regarding Skattebo’s backflips. Fans have come to wince at the thought ever since the gruesome ankle injury that ended his rookie season.He famously botched a backflip shortly before the start of training camp, spurring calls for him to retire the celebration before camp even started. At the time, the risk seemed minimal. After all, over-rotating and landing on his butt was a sign that he was generating more force than anticipated. Funny, but ultimately harmless — and even positive, from a certain perspective. But Hutchinson’s injury drove the point home, and the flips are no more. Maybe he can borrow a touchdown celebration from another football caveman and adopt the Gronk Power Spike.

title: Commanders, Cowboys get help from schedule in effort to chase down the Giants
summary: The New York Giants are leading the NFC East after 10 weeks of play, but the gap is closing. The Dallas Cowboys and Washington Commanders are hoping to take them down. There likely will only be one team coming out of the division for the playoffs, and the Giants want to make sure they are […]
full_text: ) The New York Giants are leading the NFC East after 10 weeks of play, but the gap is closing. The Dallas Cowboys and Washington Commanders are hoping to take them down. There likely will only be one team coming out of the division for the playoffs, and the Giants want to make sure they are the ones that come out on top. Here’s a look at each team’s remaining schedule and how difficult it will be for each team to navigate. Dallas Cowboys (.477, 25th-toughest in NFL) Current standing: 4–6, second place in NFC East Remaining opponents: Titans, Eagles, at Seahawks, at Rams, Jaguars, Giants, at Commanders The Cowboys have one of the easier remaining schedules in the league, but they remain in second place in the division behind the Giants. They have very winnable games coming up, with the Titans and Eagles on deck, but then things get more difficult with the Seahawks, Rams, and Jaguars before the rematch against the Giants at AT&T Stadium later in the season. That three-game stretch before that rematch against the Giants could knock them out. Some wins against some powerful teams will likely keep them in the hunt and give them some momentum before facing the Giants in their first game of the 2027 calendar year. Washington Commanders (.467, 26th-toughest in NFL) Current standing: 3-5-1, third place in NFC East Remaining opponents: Bengals, at Cardinals, at Titans, Texans, Falcons, at Vikings, at Jaguars, Cowboys The Commanders’ win against the Giants on Thursday Night Football last week kept their season alive, and their schedule is about to get easier. After this week’s Monday Night Football game against the Bengals, the schedule gets much easier for the Commanders. They will play four consecutive games against teams that don’t have a better record than them, which could lead into a run leading up to the end of the season. The final three games are a bit more challenging, as they face two likely playoff teams on the road before finishing the season against the Cowboys in a game that could decide the division if the Giants fold in the second half of the year. New York Giants (.566, fourth-toughest in NFL) Current standing: 5-3-1, No. 3 seed Remaining opponents: Jaguars, at Colts, 49ers, at Seahawks, Browns, at Lions, at Cowboys, Eagles The Giants have one of the toughest schedules remaining in the league, as only three teams will face a more challenging gauntlet in the second half of the season. With seven games to go, four come against teams that are likely heading to the playoffs. If they were to lose all four of those games, they would need to sweep the Colts, Cowboys, and Eagles in order to get to eight wins. That might be enough to win the NFC East this year, but it is far from a guarantee. The Giants should want to beat some of these top teams to give them reason to believe that they can compete in the playoffs. That all starts with this weekend’s contest against the Jaguars, which is arguably the team’s toughest test to date. Kickoff between the Jags and Giants is scheduled for Sunday at 4:25 p.m. inside MetLife Stadium. Fans can watch the game on CBS or stream it on the Paramount+ app.

title: Giants-Jaguars matchup: Jacksonville defense will look familiar
summary: The New York Giants return to action in Week 11 when they take on the Jacksonville Jaguars.. The 5-3-1 Giants enter the game as 5.5-point underdogs at home against the 7-2 Jaguars, per FanDuel. The Giants are coming off of a frustrating, and potentially significant, loss to the Washington Commanders in Week 10, while the […]
full_text: The New York Giants’ offense huddles before a play. | Getty Images The New York Giants return to action in Week 11 when they take on the Jacksonville Jaguars.. The 5-3-1 Giants enter the game as 5.5-point underdogs at home against the 7-2 Jaguars, per FanDuel . The Giants are coming off of a frustrating, and potentially significant, loss to the Washington Commanders in Week 10, while the Jaguars are riding a 3-game winning streak that features performances of 42, 33, and 40 points. The Giants are entering the toughest stretch of their schedule, and this game is believed to be an early litmus test to see if they have what it takes to hang with the best the NFL has to offer. The last time the Giants were significant underdogs, they responded by outplaying the Houston Texans and delivering a stunning upset following a bad loss to the Saints. Can the Giants’ offense respond to the loss to the Commanders and keep pace with one of the most prolific units in the NFL? Stats that matter The Jaguars’ scheme The Jacksonville Jaguars aren’t a team the Giants see all that often, and this is the first time they’ve faced off with Liam Coen as head coach and Anthony Camponile calling the defense. So with that in mind, the best place to start is with an overview of the type of defense the Giants will be facing. And in that, the Jags are more familiar than we might have expected. In fact, the schedule makers have done the Giants a low-key favor by making this game after the Eagles and Commanders. That’s because Camponile has spent time under both Vic Fangio and Brian Flores and runs a hybrid defense that incorporates elements of both schemes. The Jaguars run a high rate of Cover 3, Cover 4, and Cover 6 shells, much like the Eagles. And like Fangio, Camponile likes to use sophisticated coverage rotations to move between looks and shells after the snap. As we’ve seen with the Eagles and Fangio’s various acolytes around the NFL, the sophisticated rotations are a good way to both limit explosive plays and help create pressure passively. The rotations help confuse quarterbacks and keep the ball in their hands, giving pass rushers time to work. At the same time, the use of stunts, twists, and simulated pressures confuses blocking schemes and wastes blockers, creating advantageous match-ups elsewhere. The Jaguars start the above play in a classic Cover 4 shell, but walk a safety down to cover the slot just before the snap. Combined with the field-side cornerback (bottom of the screen) taking inside leverage, that clues us that they’re actually playing a Cover 3. The Jaguars respect the Texans’ play-action, with a fifth defender coming downhill to gap out the potential run, while the second level defenders freeze. The play design is also able to hold the free safety, keeping him from getting to the vertical route in time. The play is a big gain for Houston, but only because the protection holds up and C.J. Stroud is able to layer the ball over the trailing defender and put it where only Nico Collins can make the play. The Jaguars’ blitz rate is on par with the “Fangio Adjacent” defenses in the NFL at just 23.7% (10th-lowest). But when Camponile he does blitz, he uses similar structures as Brian Flores. Flores builds the blitz into every aspect of his defense, showing heavy pressure to gap-out the offense in the run game while creating uncertainty as to which defenders are — or are not — rushing. This play shows the other side of the Jaguars’ defense. There’s significant milling around the line of scrimmage, with all but three defenders crowding the tackle box. It’s almost impossible to know at the snap who’s rushing, who isn’t, or what coverage is even being called. They ultimately drop into a split-field coverage and there’s an opportunity for an explosive play down the sideline. However, the pressure and confusion force the ball out on the hot-read before Ward has a chance to see the open man down the field. Can J.J. McCarthy stay explosive? One of the biggest aspects the switch to J.J. McCarthy at quarterback has been unlocking the explosive elements to the Giants’ passing game. That could be significant in this game because, as Gus Logue of Big Cat Country tells us , the Jaguars have been hurt by explosive passes in the past. They’re currently the sixth-worst defense in the league in defending explosive passes (+0.82 EPA/play), despite playing the likes of the Indianapolis Colts, Baltimore Ravens, and Tennessee Titans over the past three weeks. None of those teams are offensive juggernauts this year, and while that doesn’t mean the Jaguars are a paper tiger (no pun intended), there might be an opportunity to exploit. Right now, McCarthy leads the NFL with an average of 10.4 air yards per pass while still having a good-enough completion percentage of 64.7. For context, Joe Burrow has a completion percentage of 66.4 percent, but is only averaging 7.4 air yards on his passes. And while some of McCarthy’s aggressiveness downfield has been due to third-and-long situations, he’s still been very willing to attack downfield. QB Time To Throw & Average Depth Of Target over last 6 weeks pic.twitter.com/uM5O6Fxqle — Jrfortgang (@throwthedamball) November 17, 2026 The Giants have speed on their offense to threaten defenses vertically. Malik Nabers is the Giants’ go-to receiver down the field, but they’ve also used Darnell Mooney and Malachi Fields to attack the perimeter. They’ve also recently begun using Jalin Hyatt as a “sacrificial X” receiver, sprinting down the field to force defenses to respect the vertical aspect. McCarthy has attempted deep passes to Hyatt twice now, each time just failing to connect for a big play, and it could be worth going to that well again. The Giants don’t want to live on deep, low-percentage throws. Doing so will keep their offense volatile and unsustainable. However, they’re going to need to be as aggressive as possible in this game to score touchdowns. Not only do questions (or outright concerns) about placekicker Dominic Zvada remain, but the other side of the ball sees a Jaguars’ offense that is among the best red zone offenses in the league, going against a Giants’ defense that’s one of the league’s worst in the red zone. The Giants can not force their defense to try and win the game single-handed, which means hitting their explosive plays whenever they can get (or create) the opportunity. Run the ball, or at least simulate a run game The Giants have done much better running the ball since getting Cam Skattebo more involved. Skattebo had a career day against the Houston Texans in Week 7 and ran well against the Commanders after returning from his hamstring injury, with a combined 202 yards and three touchdowns in those two games. The Giants should remain committed to their identity as a running team. However, they should also be willing to extend the running game if they aren’t finding room around the line of scrimmage with the arrival of Jordan Davis and Davon Godcheaux on the Jaguars’ defensive front. Skattebo had 121 total yards against the Texans, and 122 total yards against the Commanders, which includes a combined 41 receiving yards. Skattebo, Devin Singletary, and Gregory Desrosiers all have upside (in different forms) as receiving threats out of the backfield. And while the Jaguars’ blitz packages could frustrate their pass protection as well as running game, there could be opportunities to use the backs to replace the blitzing defenders and keep the offense on schedule. Using their running backs as receiving threats is also a potentially useful deviation from their usual tendencies. The Giants love to use 22-personnel packages with two backs and two tight ends on the field. Personnel usage by team has a few major outliers: – Raiders: lowest 11 and highest 12 personnel rates in the league – Rams: Most 13 personnel by 11 points – 49ers/Chargers/Dolphins: 2-back sets galore, especially 21 personnel – Giants: 22 personnel on 19% of plays,…

title: ‘5 questions’ about the Jacksonville Jaguars: Is it Super Bowl or bust?
summary: The Jacksonville Jaguars will be the best team the New York Giants have faced this season when the teams meet on Sunday. Let’s learn more about the Jaguars in this week’s ‘5 questions’ segment. Gus Logue of SB Nation’s Big Cat Country provides our answers. Ed: The Jaguars, obviously, went all-in to improve the roster […]
full_text: The Jacksonville Jaguars will be the best team the New York Giants have faced this season when the teams meet on Sunday. Let’s learn more about the Jaguars in this week’s ‘5 questions’ segment. Gus Logue of SB Nation’s Big Cat Country provides our answers. Ed: The Jaguars, obviously, went all-in to improve the roster at the trade deadline. After going 13-4 a season and being that aggressive at the deadline, has this become a year where anything less than a Super Bowl appearance makes the season a disappointment? Gus: At this point, anything less than a Super Bowl victory would be disappointing for the 2026 Jaguars. The new regime has been “strategically bold,” making aggressive and unorthodox moves to bolster a well-balanced roster that already boasts a great quarterback and an even better coaching staff. Jags fans appreciate that the team is genuinely trying to win it all, especially after so many seasons in the gutter, rather than letting this opportunity slip by. Jacksonville’s moves at the trade deadline do fall in the “win now” bucket but I wouldn’t necessarily categorize it as an “all-in” approach. The Jaguars will be contenders for the next several seasons — not just for 2026. Ed: If I gave you the option of taking Trevor Lawrence or any other current quarterback in the NFL, would you keep Lawrence? If not, who would you take? Gus: I would definitely take Patrick Mahomes. A few other quarterbacks can match his playmaking ability from both inside and outside the pocket, but nobody does it like him in clutch moments. Josh Allen and a healthy Lamar Jackson would probably still clear Lawrence, but if I were tiering quarterbacks, I’d have a “Zeus” category for Mahomes, an “Olympians” category for Allen, Jackson, Lawrence, Joe Burrow, Drake Maye, and Caleb Williams, and maybe a “demigods” tier for guys like Jaxson Dart and J.J. McCarthy who have shown special flashes but aren’t yet considered football deities. I have zero qualms with how Lawrence is playing the position right now. Ed: If you could take one player off the Giants’ roster and put him into Jacksonville’s lineup, who would it be? Why? Gus: The idea of Malik Nabers in Liam Coen’s offense makes me salivate, and the thought of Arvell Reese in Anthony Campanile’s defense gives me goosebumps. I might’ve said Jevon Holland before Jacksonville traded for Jessie Bates III last week. Andrew Thomas would probably be the responsible choice. But I will go with Abdul Carter, who would arguably provide the most game-changing plays for Jacksonville. Josh Hines-Allen and Travon Walker already occupy the starting edge positions, and the team is looking forward to second-year pro B.J. Green II returning from injured reserve, but another pass rusher could not hurt. Once the team starts seeing elite quarterbacks each week in January, it’d be handy to have a guy like Carter. Ed: Tell us about one offensive and one defensive player Giants fans should be paying attention to on Sunday? Gus: On offense, look out for Parker Washington. This kid isn’t just a fun little success story as a former sixth-round pick who first carved out a role on special teams. At least not anymore. Washington has blossomed into a borderline top-10 NFL wide receiver and the unquestioned engine of Jacksonville’s offense. The Penn State product will be more widely recognized in the tri-state area after this weekend. On the other side of the ball, look out for fourth-year linebacker Ventrell Miller. The former Gator has filled in wonderfully after offseason 2025 Pro Bowler Devin Lloyd departed in the offseason. Miller plays like a missile against the run. Ed: What is the Jaguars Kryptonite? On offense? Defense? If the Giants are going to win the game, how and what do they need to attack? Gus: The Jaguars’ biggest weakness is its offensive line. It’s been a “good enough” unit for most of the season, but the teams that pose the biggest threat to Jacksonville are those with a dominant front four that controls the line of scrimmage. If you can shut down the Jaguars’ running game and constantly heat up Lawrence, you’ll have a shot. On defense, the Jaguars allow the lowest EPA/play on short passes (-0.23) and the fifth-lowest mark on intermediate passes (-0.1), but they rank sixth-worst against deep passes (+0.82). Bates was brought in to help clean that up, and Travis Hunter gets better every week, but Jacksonville has to do a better job of limiting explosive passes — even if they’re not allowing many such attempts in the first place. The Jaguars have the horses to contain Cam Skattebo but they should be wary of Nabers and New York’s front seven.

full_text: Nikko Reed with the Chargers. | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The New York Giants are reportedly signing cornerback Nikko Reed , who was dropped from the 53-man roster on Monday, to their practice squad. Reed takes the place of running back Eric Gray , who was released from the practice squad on Tuesday. Reed, 23, was signed off the Los Angeles Chargers’ practice squad on Sept. 19. He played in three games for the Giants, exclusively on special teams. He made one tackle. Reed was cut on Monday when the Giants signed veteran special teams player and defensive back Tavierre Thomas off the Minnesota Vikings’ practice squad. Gray was a fifth-round pick by the Giants in 2023. He played in 34 games for the Giants over three seasons, with 31 carries for 79 yards rushing, 2.5 yards per attempt. Gray was released when the Giants cut their roster to 53 players before the season started, but was re-signed to the practice squad two weeks ago.

title: 5 NY Giants-Jacksonville Jaguars storylines: Time to step up in class
summary: The calendar says mid-November, and the New York Giants are playing meaningful games at this time of year for the first time since 2022. Let’s look at some of the storylines for Sunday’s matchup at MetLife Stadium against the Jacksonville Jaguars. Entering the heavyweight division When the two teams line up on Sunday, it will […]
full_text: The calendar says mid-November, and the New York Giants are playing meaningful games at this time of year for the first time since 2022. Let’s look at some of the storylines for Sunday’s matchup at MetLife Stadium against the Jacksonville Jaguars. Entering the heavyweight division When the two teams line up on Sunday, it will mark the first time this season the Giants will look across the field at a team with a winning record. The 6-4 Los Angeles Rams are currently the only winning team the Giants have faced, but the Rams were 0-1 when the teams met. Los Angeles won that game, 28-6. The Giants lost quarterback Jaxson Dart seven plays into that game, so perhaps that blowout is not indicative of how the Giants stack up. Five of the Giants’ final eight games this season are against teams with winning records. Whether they win on Sunday or not, how competitive the Giants are might tell us a lot about how well or how poorly the remainder of the season might go for the NFC East division leaders. Kick return merry-go-round Gunner Olszwewski was expected to be the Giants’ primary punt and kickoff returner. Only, he suffered a torn Achilles in training camp. Braxton Berrios got that spot, and suffered a season-ending foot injury after four games. Along came Charlie Jones. This week, after some ball security issues, out went Jones. The Giants have also lost Tryone Tracy, who has been their best kickoff returner, for a few weeks with a hamstring injury. They have tried Devin Singletary on kickoff returns, but he doesn’t really have the speed to succeed in that role. They have tried rookie Gregory Desrosiers, but he fumbled a return last week against the Washington Commanders. Now, along comes Xavier Gipson as the replacement for Jones. Gipson is in his third tour with the Giants, though he has never played a game for them. He has career averages of 9.1 yards returning punts and 25.9 yards returning kickoffs. That’s good. His 12 fumbles in 163 career touches, one every 13.6 touches, is bad. Jones had become an adventure in recent weeks. The Giants felt they had to try something different, but there is no guarantee that Gipson will be any better. One thing to watch: As the games get more important, might the Giants use starting cornerback Deonte Banks on kickoff returns? Banks was fantastic in that role last season, averaging 32.7 yards on 19 returns, including a 95-yard touchdown. He was, however, only a part-time defensive player last season. Now, he is probably the Giants’ best cornerback. ‘Hold on to that ball, Petey!’ That is one of the famous lines from the movie ‘ Remember the Titans ’. Holding on to the ball is something the Giants need to learn how to do. The Giants have 17 fumbles in nine games. Only the Green Bay Packers, who have played 10 games, have more with 18. The Giants and 1-8 Los Angeles Chargers average a league-worst 1.9 fumbles per game. It should be obvious that the Giants are going to have a difficult time beating top-tier teams if their ballcarriers keep putting the ball on the ground. By the way, the National Weather Service says there is a 40% chance of rain in East Rutherford, N.J. on Sunday. Adventures of the right hashmark Giants’ owner John Mara has a fair amount of power in league circles. Can he use it to push through an emergency rule change that placekickers get to choose which hashmark they kick from on field goals as well as extra points? Dominic Zvada and the Giants’ playoff hopes would appreciate it. By now, it has been well-documented that all six of Zvada’s missed field goals this season have come from the right hashmark . In all seriousness, the Giants need to hope Zvada has that issue figured out by Sunday. Turn up the heat, Dennard Giants’ defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson has been throwing caution to the wind and dialing up the heat in recent weeks. Three times since Week 4, Wilson has called for the blitz on more than 50% of passing downs. Only once in that stretch has he blitzed less than on 40% of passing downs. Overall, NextGen Stats has the Giants blitzing on 40.6% of passing snaps. Only the Minnesota Vikings (a ridiculous 72.3%), Tampa Bay Buccaneers (43.9%), and Washington Commanders (42.1%) have blitzed more. This shapes up as one of those weeks when dictating to Jaguars’ quarterback Trevor Lawrence seems like a good idea. title: The Jets Need To Reimagine Their Running Back Usage
summary: I’ll start this article with a shameless pat on the back. Despite me getting numerous things wrong throughout the years (likely more wrong than right), one thing I’ve been very happy to see develop is the breakout of Braelon Allen. Now, for those who know my opinion on the matter, you know I’ve been pretty […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - AUGUST 09: Breece Hall #20 and Braelon Allen #0 of the New York Jets warm up prior to the game against the Green Bay Packers during the NFL Preseason 2025 game between New York Jets and Green Bay Packers at Lambeau Field on August 09, 2025 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Justin Casterline/Getty Images) | Getty Images I’ll start this article with a shameless pat on the back. Despite me getting numerous things wrong throughout the years (likely more wrong than right), one thing I’ve been very happy to see develop is the breakout of Braelon Allen. Now, for those who know my opinion on the matter, you know I’ve been pretty vocal about Allen’s potential and what he could end up being. It was rooted in a pretty simple theory: Allen is too strong, big, and fast to fail. If I had to get into a bit more detail, I could talk about how Allen possesses great contact balance, is light on his feet, showcases strong vision, and does all of this while being extremely young (he was 17 as a true freshman and just 20 when he entered the league). One of the few positive developments for the Jets this year was just how effective Allen was when Breece Hall was injured. Look at some of these snaps just the week prior to Breece’s return: Braelon Allen explosive runs vs Raiders pic.twitter.com/slf2ppAp0c — Omari Brown (@OmariiBrown) November 2, 2026 Come on, this is some good stuff. However, like most things with the Jets, it got complicated once Breece Hall returned. What would be a great problem to have for certain teams, two good players at the same position who complement each other well, has already become a big-time headache for the Jets. How does the staff utilize the skill sets of Breece Hall and Braelon Allen effectively? How can they both contribute as difference-makers to this team while still getting enough opportunities? Now, it’s a small sample since Breece Hall has come back (only two games), but I’m going to make my case as to why the early usage split doesn’t make much sense to me. Usage From a distance, I think everyone is probably in agreement that, simply put, Braelon Allen has flashed more as a runner this year. Before we even get to the stats, I think I could get most people to agree with that just from watching the two play. Allen fits your typical profile of a heavy-usage back. He’s big, has good vision, can break tackles, and rarely gets tackled for a loss. Breece is a bit different. Down by down, he’ll leave you with some inconsistencies. He’s heavily reliant on his breakaway speed, but that also makes him incredibly effective in the open field. He’s got a history of turning small gains into explosive ones. A stat I remember from this offseason really reminds me of this. Since 2020, there’s only been one player with 3+ 50-yard runs and 3+ 50-yard receptions in that time frame: Breece Hall. But now, let’s take a look at some of the rushing stats from this year. We’ll use a few metrics from Next Gen Stats that help demonstrate how Allen has been significantly more impactful as a down-to-down runner. Here are some of the metrics we’ll be looking at: Efficiency (EFF): Rushing efficiency is calculated by taking the total distance a player traveled on rushing plays as a ball carrier, according to Next Gen Stats, and dividing it by the rushing yards gained. The lower the number, the more of a north-south runner the player is. 8+ Defenders in the Box (8+D%): On every play, Next Gen Stats calculates how many defenders are stacked in the box at the snap. Using that logic, this metric calculates how often a rusher sees eight or more defenders in the box against them. Average Time Behind the Line of Scrimmage (TLOS): Next Gen Stats measures the amount of time a ball carrier spends behind the line of scrimmage before crossing it, measured to the nearest tenth of a second. TLOS represents the average time behind the LOS on all rushing plays where the player is the rusher. Rushing Yards Over Expected (RYOE): The difference between actual yards gained and expected yards gained (Actual – Expected). This uses player tracking data, including the position, speed, and direction of the runner, blockers, and defenders at the moment of handoff, to calculate how many yards an average running back would gain in that exact scenario. A positive number means the runner created yardage beyond what the blocking and defensive alignment provided. Rushing Over Expected Percentage (ROE%): Also tracked as Carries Beating Expected (%), this measures the share of a runner’s carries that gain more yardage than the NFL Next Gen Stats Expected Rushing Yards model predicts. While total RYOE can be skewed by a single massive breakout run, ROE% highlights down-to-down consistency. Now, let’s compare: Breece Hall: 77 carries, 265 yards, 3.4 AVG 4.8 EFF 2.79 TLOS -31 RYOE 32% ROE Braelon Allen: 128 carries, 638 yards, 5.0 AVG 3.41 EFF 2.72 TLOS 118 RYOE 52% ROE So, what do these stats tell us? A few things. For starters, they show that Breece has been significantly less of a north-south runner than Braelon Allen has. Hall actually has the 5th highest EFF in the league, showing that he’s traveling a lot of distance on plays without getting much to show for it. That also shows up in his RYOE and ROE numbers. He ranks in the bottom 10 in ROE%, something Hall has historically struggled with due to his home-run running style. He’s actually performed worse than what would be expected from an average back and that’s shown with the -31 RYOE. To Breece’s credit, he’s normally better than this. He may have been hampered by the injury earlier this year. Again, he has a tendency to make up for some of these inconsistencies with a handful of explosive runs. But the numbers this year have been pretty telling. Allen, though, has been quite frankly terrific. He’s top 8 in RYOE and yards per carry this year. He hasn’t showcased the historic explosiveness that Hall has, but Allen actually ranks #1 in the league in ROE%. That shows that Allen is rarely leaving yards on the field. He doesn’t have the home-run ability Hall has, and probably never will, but if you need a workhorse back who consistently churns out positive yards, keeps the offense above the sticks, and prevents the team from getting into bad situations, there legitimately hasn’t been a better back in the NFL at that this year than Allen. But the running back position isn’t just about running. We also have to consider how each back performs on passing downs. From a pass-protection perspective, there’s not a ton to glean from the numbers. Hall has historically graded decently in most metrics. He’s never been great, but he’s usually around average by PFF grade and ranks 19th out of 60 backs this year. He’s not a liability. Allen, quietly, has been great in this regard according to PFF. In an extremely small sample last year, his grade would have been good enough to finish as a top-2 back. This year, he ranks 6th in PFF grade. Based on what we’ve seen over the last season and a half, it’s probably fair to say Allen is a well above-average pass protector. Now, what about receiving? This is where Hall has the clear advantage, both in the stats and on film. Let’s take a look: Breece Hall: 17 catches, 18 targets, 195 yards 2.71 Yards Per Route Run 6 Missed Tackles Forced 8 First Downs Braelon Allen: 20 catches, 24 targets, 108 yards 0.68 Yards Per Route Run 6 Missed Tackles Forced 6 First Downs What does this data show? Hall is far, far better as a pass-catcher. And while the yards per route run number will likely normalize (it’s better than 95% of NFL wide receivers right now), Hall has consistently been a more than effective pass-catcher throughout his career. His career yards per route run is 1.59, a very good pace for a running back. For context, Jahmyr Gibbs sits at 1.56 yards per route run in his career. Christian McCaffrey and Alvin Kamara, probably the two best backs in recent memory at catching passes out of the…

summary: The New York Jets have solicited advice from nearly everyone on planet Earth when hiring head coaches this century. full_text: PITTSBURGH, PA - OCTOBER 21: Quarterback Peyton Manning #18 of the Indianapolis Colts talks on a telephone to coaches sitting overhead as he looks on from the sideline during a game against the Pittsburgh Steelers at Heinz Field on October 21, 2002 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. That has included The 33rd Team, Charley Casserly, and do you remember that one time when Pro Football Hall of Famer Peyton Manning made a phone call to seal the deal for Adam Gase? Great times. That can’t happen in 2027. Make no mistake about it: the Jets will be looking for a new head coach in a matter of months, but in all of those other situations, they lost the battle before it ever began. Stop relying on people outside of the building. Put your big boy pants on and make a decision for yourself. Who is the right man for that job? Darren Mougey. Woody Johnson has called Mougey “The General” this offseason when referencing him to fans. He has spoken highly of him and believes the team is going in the right direction because of Mougey. Put him in the driver’s seat for this search and allow him to vet the candidates. ESPN New York’s Jake Asman called the latest Jets HC search a “sham” on the “Jets Collective” podcast. “Woody Johnson put Mike Tannenbaum, Rick Spielman, and The 33rd Team in charge of vetting candidates. Liam Coen is a UMass alum, Mike Tannenbaum went to UMass, and again, I work with Mike, so I’m comfortable saying this to his face. We’ve had many battles on the air and off the air, but if [the] Coz reporting is right that they got the intel wrong on Liam Coen, it’s another indictment of just this sham of a search process that led to Aaron Glenn.” J-E-T-S! title: Eagles claim Cowboys draft pick off waivers
summary: The Philadelphia Eagles claimed Ajani Cornelius off waivers from the Dallas Cowboys, according to an official team announcement. Cornelius, 24, is a 6-5, 318 pound offensive lineman who was selected with a sixth-round pick (No. 204 overall) in the 2025 NFL Draft. Playing college football for Rhode Island and Oregon, Cornelius almost exclusively played at […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - OCTOBER 26: Ajani Cornelius #65 of the Dallas Cowboys exits the field during an NFL football game against the Philadelphia Eagles at Lincoln Financial Field on October 26, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Perry Knotts/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Philadelphia Eagles claimed Ajani Cornelius off waivers from the Dallas Cowboys, according to an official team announcement. Cornelius, 24, is a 6-5, 318 pound offensive lineman who was selected with a sixth-round pick (No. 204 overall) in the 2025 NFL Draft. Playing college football for Rhode Island and Oregon, Cornelius almost exclusively played at right tackle. Pre-draft scouting report via NFL.com : A durable lineman with NFL traits and four years of starting experience, Cornelius lacks standout flashes on tape. He has been a full-time right tackle but lacks protection talent to stay outside as a pro. He has access to physical tools but needs to play with better bend and hand quickness to help stabilize his play. He can cover up defenders with size but is frequently out-leveraged at the point of attack. His average body control and slide quickness should be mitigated in smaller spaces but those issues will still be concerning against explosive interior rushers. The traits should make him a Day 3 target, but his ceiling might be as a backup. During his time with Dallas, Cornelius logged zero offensive snaps and 21 special teams snaps over four regular season games played. He played at right tackle during the 2025 preseason before the Cowboys moved him to right guard in the 2026 preseason. The Eagles seem to think Cornelius has some developmental potential. It also makes sense for them to add some more offensive tackle depth after waiving Fred Johnson. As an added bonus, the Eagles might’ve snagged a player the Cowboys were hoping to get back on their practice squad.

full_text: Jul 29, 2026; Oxnard, CA, USA; Dallas Cowboys defensive coordinator Christian Parker at training camp at River Ridge Playing Fields. Mandatory Credit: Kirby Lee-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Back on October 13, we noted how Christian Parker seemed to be getting Sean Desai’d with the Dallas Cowboys bringing Mike Pettine in as a defensive assistant. That prophecy has now fully come to fruition with Parker losing play-calling duty to Pettine . It’s not hard to understand why the Cowboys are making this move; Dallas has the worst defense in the NFL. They just allowed 46 points and 584 yards in a home loss to the San Francisco 49ers. The Cowboys are looking for a spark that can get them pointed in the right direction with the NFC East crown still within reach. The Desai change famously didn’t work well for the Eagles in 2023. Their defense was even worse under Matt Patricia. But the Cowboys don’t really have any room to go but up from here. On one hand, it’s funny to watch the Cowboys scramble like this. On the other hand, it’s unfortunate that Parker — a contributor to the Eagles’ Super Bowl LIX victory — is floundering and now being publicly embarrassed by being demoted. It would probably be more respectful for the Cowboys to fire him as opposed to keeping up this charade where he’s the defensive coordinator in title only.

title: How do the Steelers stack up in the AFC playoff picture?
summary: Following an embarrassing performance against the rival Bengals in primetime, it’s safe to say that the energy in the Steelers fanbase has once again returned to biblical levels of doom and gloom. And it’s hard to blame anyone for feeling that way. After putting together their most well-rounded and physically imposing victory of their own […]
full_text: Photo by Jeff Dean/Getty Images | Getty Images Following an embarrassing performance against the rival Bengals in primetime, it’s safe to say that the energy in the Steelers fanbase has once again returned to biblical levels of doom and gloom. And it’s hard to blame anyone for feeling that way. After putting together their most well-rounded and physically imposing victory of their own against the Browns before the bye, it’s been a bitter dose of reality in the days since the team’s 38-18 loss to Cincinnati, in which most well-seasoned Steelers fans could tell the game was all but over after a first quarter in which Pittsburgh possessed the ball for barely a minute. Before the season, this column predicted that the Steelers would win roughly 10 games, make the playoffs, and potentially win one postseason game if they landed a favorable matchup. And while the Steelers certainly did not feel like a serious team at any point during Sunday Night Football, it’s worth pointing out that they are still on track to make the postseason. Looking at the AFC playoff picture on the NFL’s website, the Steelers have a projected 73% chance of making the playoffs. The field for the AFC seems narrowed and set, barring any insane collapses and/or turnarounds. Of the nine teams currently outside of playoff positioning, six of them have three wins or fewer. Two of the remaining three teams are likely without their starting quarterback for the rest of the regular season at minimum (Patriots, Ravens), and the third just turned to a rookie quarterback with a tough schedule remaining (Raiders). As flawed as this Steelers roster may be, it is still more likely than not that they’ll be playing in the Wild Card round. So while the timing might feel off based on the collective bad vibes we’re feeling, Sunday’s loss makes the following conversation feel that more relevant. We ranked the top eight non-Steelers team in the AFC playoff picture/bubble based on the criteria: Who could Pittsburgh realistically beat in a playoff game? Bills Difficulty ranking: RB – 1, RP – 2 Current AFC No. 1 seed; >99% playoff chance per NFL.com RB : Is this finally the Bills’ year? Buffalo’s struggles to get over the hump to the Super Bowl have been well-documented, but Josh Allen and co.’s ability to win in the Wild Card round (6-1, including a 2024 victory over Pittsburgh) has not been a problem. The Bills are a juggernaut on offense, ranking first in points per game, fourth in yards, and third in EPA. What always flies under the radar is how Buffalo can win in a number of ways, with the league’s second-ranked rushing offense led by James Cook, along with a 13th-ranked passing offense led by perpetual MVP candidate Josh Allen. (The Bills would rank much higher if they threw more, currently third in yards per pass play and fifth in EPA per pass). However, the Bills still have some proving to do despite a near-perfect 8-1 record, having given up 30-plus points four times already this season en route to a 28th-ranked passing defense. Still the Bills rank middle of the pack in points per game allowed (15) and top 10 against the run (eighth). They have an underrated front and have allowed just 28 points over the last three games, although it has been against the Jets, Vikings and Ravens. Buffalo fits in that tier of teams where it’s hard to imagine Pittsburgh keeping up if a game turned into a shootout. And the Bills’ defense’s strength being against the run just makes things tougher for a Steelers team that needs to get the ground game going to succeed. Jaguars Difficulty ranking: RB – 2, RP – 1 Current AFC No. 3 seed; >99% playoff chance per NFL.com RP : The Jaguars were my preseason pick to represent the AFC in the Super Bowl, and that feeling has only increased for me since then. With respect to Josh Allen and the Bills, the team from Duval gets my vote for most difficult matchup, largely because I believe them to be the most well-balanced team in the conference this year. Whether you’re a fan of modern analytics or more traditional stats, this Jaguars club favors well. They are ranked fourth in both offensive EPA per play (+0.10) and opponent EPA allowed per play (-0.18). They rank first in point differential (+125). They score the fourth-most points per game (29.9) while allowing the fourth-fewest (16.0). And they are both ninth in total yards per game gained (358.9) and allowed (319.2). On offense, this team motions receivers at the NFL’s fourth-highest rate (75%) to create favorable matchups, and then they’re bombs away with the highest frequency of passes traveling over 10 air yards (43%). On defense, the Jaguars live in base defense (4-3) at a higher rate (52%) than all but three teams. They don’t blitz a ton, but still generate a high rate of pressure. Long story short, the Jaguars have the type of offense that can give the Pittsburgh secondary fits, while still winning enough on the ground. On defense, the Jaguars rely on a base defensive look that can counterpunch the Steelers’ running game while still smothering the passing game. We’ll dive into this team in further detail when these teams play in Week 14, but suffice it to say, this is a scary matchup for Pittsburgh. Chiefs Difficulty ranking: RB – 3, RP – 4 Current AFC No. 2 seed; 97% playoff chance per NFL.com. RB : The Chiefs are largely back after a disastrous 2025, currently ranking as the AFC’s No. 2 seed with a 7-2 record. That’s scary news for the rest of the NFL, as the head coach/quarterback combination of Andy Reid and Patrick Mahomes has far more postseason experience and success than the rest of the field combined. The Chiefs’ offense, top 10 in both points and yards this season, has Mahomes averaging eight yards per attempt for the first time since 2022, even if he still isn’t pushing the ball down the field much. And the addition of Kenneth Walker III, now an Offensive Player of the Year frontrunner, has given the Chiefs an elite running back for the first time in the Mahomes era. Don’t discount the recent trade for Josh Downs, either, which provided a much-needed reinforcement to KC’s group of pass catchers. The Chiefs’ defense is once again competent, in the upper half of the league against the run and pass and top six in points and EPA per play allowed. Kansas City is blitzing less than in past seasons (a 17th-ranked 30.6% this year) but coordinator Steve Spagnuolo remains one of the league’s most innovative minds when it comes to pressure, and he’s not afraid to use man coverage, either — not a great matchup for Pittsburgh. The one saving grace of facing the Chiefs for the Steelers is that a wide receiver room of Rashee Rice, Downs, and Xavier Worthy isn’t as terrifying for a reeling Pittsburgh secondary as most of the other teams on this list. But this is not a team or coaching staff you want to be facing in January. Bengals Difficulty ranking: RB – 4, RP – 3 Current AFC No. 4 seed; 98% playoff chance per NFL.com RP : We don’t need to drag this one on too long; the wounds are still fresh. As long as Joe Burrow, Ja’Marr Chase, and Tee Higgins are healthy, this matchup is a coin flip for the Steelers on the best of days, and a complete mismatch on their worst. Joe Burrow is turning in an MVP-level performance this season, despite every team knowing exactly how the Bengals plan to attack them. He can pick apart zone coverages, and the All-Worldly duo of Chase and Higgins can win matchups against man coverage more often than they lose. If secondary weapons like Chase Brown and Mike Gesicki bring their A-games to a contest, it’s all the worse for the opposing defense. The Bengals defense is still streaky. The defensive line is currently its strength, but the linebackers are gettable in both phases, and the secondary lives and dies by the pass rush’s performance. Bryan Cook and Jordan Battle are an above-average safety tandem this year, but the cornerbacks have been up and down. The Bengals’ defense is also pretty terrible…

title: Steelers place Mason McCormick on injured reserve
summary: The Steelers got good news regarding offensive lineman Mason McCormick early Wednesday, with the starting left guard suffering a dislocated ankle instead of a fracture — avoiding surgery after a gruesome-looking injury on Sunday versus the Bengals. However, McCormick will still be missing the Steelers’ next four games at minimum, with the team placing him […]
full_text: Photo by Ian Johnson/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Steelers got good news regarding offensive lineman Mason McCormick early Wednesday, with the starting left guard suffering a dislocated ankle instead of a fracture — avoiding surgery after a gruesome-looking injury on Sunday versus the Bengals. However, McCormick will still be missing the Steelers’ next four games at minimum, with the team placing him on injured reserve Wednesday, Pittsburgh announced . With McCormick now on IR, the Steelers have an opening on their 53-man roster. After Pittsburgh opened the 21-day practice window for wide receivers Michael Pittman Jr. and Roman Wilson, as well as rookie guard Gennings Dunker, earlier in the day, the team could leave the vacant spot available for one of those three players’ eventual activation. Steelers utility lineman Spencer Anderson is expected to start at left guard for the team while McCormick misses time. The earliest McCormick can return to the lineup would be the Steelers’ Dec. 20 matchup against the Baltimore Ravens, although a report from NFL Network’s Ian Rapoport on Wednesday indicated the Steelers hope McCormick can return for the playoffs, which don’t begin until mid-January.

title: Steelers open practice window for Michael Pittman Jr, Roman Wilson
summary: The Pittsburgh Steelers suffered their most embarrassing loss of the season on Sunday Night Football to the Cincinnati Bengals in Week 10, with the Bengals gaining control of first place in the AFC North. But with the division and playoffs still very much in reach for the Steelers, they got great news on Wednesday with […]
full_text: Photo by Jeff Dean/Getty Images | Getty Images The Pittsburgh Steelers suffered their most embarrassing loss of the season on Sunday Night Football to the Cincinnati Bengals in Week 10, with the Bengals gaining control of first place in the AFC North. But with the division and playoffs still very much in reach for the Steelers, they got great news on Wednesday with the return of four players to practice. Steelers head coach Mike McCarthy announced Wednesday that the team opened the 21-day practice window for four players: Michael Pittman Jr., Roman Wilson, Gennings Dunker, and Max Hurleman. Mike McCarthy says they’re opening the 21-day practice day windows for Michael Pittman Jr., Roman Wilson, Gennings Dunker, and Max Hurleman today. Some big news for the Steelers. — Nick Farabaugh (@FarabaughFB) November 18, 2026 Pittsburgh later announced that Hurleman was activated to the practice squad, with wide receiver Isaiah Hodgins being released to make room. Pittman Jr. returns to practice after suffering a plantar fasciitis injury that landed him on injured reserve on Oct. 10. The wide receiver was seen working off to the side last week and running with the team during warmups. He even went as far as to say that he felt healthy enough to return last week . Now he will get that chance to provide a boost to the Steelers’ receiver room. Also a boost to the room, Roman Wilson is set to return after suffering a finger injury in Week 5. Wilson and Pittman Jr.’s return should bode well for a Steelers passing game that has looked lackluster over the course of the last month. Max Hurleman is also a name to watch, after he was the subject of a lot of praise from coaches and teammates last week. After several years of string training camp performances, the team made it clear how they feel about Hurleman. Now he returns to practice and will fight for an opportunity to get a helmet on game day. After the injury to starting right guard Mason McCormick, getting Gennings Dunker back provides some nice depth. Dunker was one of the Steelers’ three third-round picks last April, and is viewed as more of a developmental player than anything. Even with his return and the injury to McCormick, fans should still expect Spencer Anderson to hold down the right guard duties. The Steelers still have to activate Pittman, Wilson and Dunker before they can play. Hurleman has been activated to the practice squad but would have to be elevated to appear in a game. Particularly for Wilson and Pittman Jr., keeping track of their participation in practice this week will be key to whether or not they play as soon as this weekend against the Philadelphia Eagles. title: Seahawks snap reactions: Dante Fowler Jr plays season-high snap share vs. Raiders
summary: The Seattle Seahawks took care of the Las Vegas Raiders on Sunday, assuring themselves of a winning record entering the bye. It was a game of few offensive snaps for both teams in what was a tale of two halves, as the Seahawks controlled the second half while the Raiders weren’t short on time with […]
full_text: The Seattle Seahawks took care of the Las Vegas Raiders on Sunday, assuring themselves of a winning record entering the bye. It was a game of few offensive snaps for both teams in what was a tale of two halves, as the Seahawks controlled the second half while the Raiders weren’t short on time with the ball in the first half. As a result, the only players who played north of 50 offensive snaps for Seattle were Drew Lock, plus every starting offensive lineman except Abe Lucas. Seattle Seahawks Week 10 offensive snap counts Seattle leaned heavily on having 12 and 13 personnel sets in this one, with Nick Kallerup managing to outsnap Rashid Shaheed even after missing the end of the game with a minor ankle injury. Shaheed’s return also meant Tory Horton was back to a distant WR4 status with only 10 snaps played. Zach Charbonnet is the clear RB1 over Jadarian Price, so there isn’t nearly the time-share deal as we saw with Kenneth Walker and Charbonnet last season. By the way, Irv Charles’ three snaps were all on Drew Lock’s kneeldowns, so don’t get too excited there. He did his work on special teams with 20 snaps. On defense, what looked to be a long day for Seattle turned into a slew of three-and-outs for Fernando Mendoza and company after halftime. The Seahawks played 59 total snaps, with safeties Julian Love and Ty Okada, cornerback Devon Witherspoon, and linebacker Ernest Jones IV going the distance. The usual suspects are atop the snap counts list. Seattle Seahawks Week 10 defensive snaps One of the biggest things that jumps out is Dante Fowler’s snap count, which went up to 20 for only the second time all season. Beyond the raw snap total, his percentage of defensive snaps played was a season-high 34 percent. Fowler made very little impact throughout the first half of the year, but sacks in consecutive games perhaps earned him more playing time. Even against the Arizona Cardinals in Week 9, Fowler was outsnapped by Mike Morris, but that was not the case this time. Uchenna Nwosu’s 27 snaps played in his return from injury is his third-lowest of the season, but his 45.8% snap share is the second-lowest ahead of Week 7 against the Kansas City Chiefs. With a bye coming up, perhaps Nwosu will ramp up and his playing time will normalize again. Lastly, Rylie Mills has played 55 total snaps over the past two games without Leonard Williams in the lineup. For perspective, he played 34 total snaps in 2025 and didn’t reach the 55-snap mark in 2026 until Week 4. He’s had his struggles throughout the year but the defensive line by no means collapsed with him getting a heavier workload. And now we take this week off and await a season-defining rematch versus the San Francisco 49ers in Week 12.

title: Tory Horton’s crucial kickoff play earns him NFC Special Teams Player of the Week
summary: The Seattle Seahawks have found themselves in several batted-ball controversies, but none broke new ground like wide receiver Tory Horton’s effort on Sunday against the Las Vegas Raiders. Horton’s bat mirrored that of a home run-robbing catch as he knocked down the Raiders’ kickoff so his teammate, Rashid Shaheed, could run the game past the […]
full_text: The Seattle Seahawks have found themselves in several batted-ball controversies, but none broke new ground like wide receiver Tory Horton’s effort on Sunday against the Las Vegas Raiders. Horton’s bat mirrored that of a home run-robbing catch as he knocked down the Raiders’ kickoff so his teammate, Rashid Shaheed, could run the game past the two-minute warning and clinch a Seahawks victory. absolutely incredible. the Raiders boom the kickoff out of the end zone to keep the 2-minute warning in play. instead, Tory Horton gets up, swats it back into the field of play, and Las Vegas is down 8 with only two timeouts and under 2 minutes to play. AWESOME. pic.twitter.com/kHqgWOr5K7 — Christian D'Andrea (@TrainIsland) November 15, 2026 For his efforts, the Seahawks special teamer was first flagged on the play, but has since been honored by the league. The Colorado State alum earned the NFC Special Teams Player of the Week Award, creating one of, if not the funniest ‘stat’ graphic of all time. NFC Players of the Week! (Week 10) @Jahmyr_Gibbs1 | @JJPhillips15 | @toryhorton11 pic.twitter.com/L8iYcdGSK3 — NFL (@NFL) November 18, 2026 The award is Horton’s first and just the latest in a string of honors for the Seahawks’ special teams group. Shaheed himself earned the player of the week award after his punt return touchdown against the Los Angeles Rams in Week 14 last season. He also becomes the first Colorado State position player to earn the award, per the NFL, which is perhaps the only thing CSU Rams fans will be able to celebrate this season. While the second-year wideout has struggled to find a consistent role in the offense, like nearly every pass catcher outside of Jaxon Smith-Njigba, he has been a core special teamer this season. Horton has filled in while Shaheed has battled injuries and recorded a 37-yard kick return against the Kansas City Chiefs. The Seahawks’ wide receiver’s tremendous play helped Seattle improve to 6-4, keeping their playoff hopes alive heading into their bye week.

full_text: A member of the Seattle Seahawks’ 2026 draft class is back, again. After being waived to begin the week , the Seahawks signed seventh-round pick Deven Eastern to their practice squad on Tuesday, the team announced. Eastern, selected with the team’s penultimate selection in this year’s draft, 242nd overall, has spent most of the season on Seattle’s practice squad after he was waived during the cut down from 90 to 53. Promoted to the active roster ahead of the Week 9 win over the Arizona Cardinals, as the Seahawks entered the game without Leonard Williams or Brandon Pili, Eastern was waived from the 53-man roster on Monday. Despite spending two weeks on the active roster, Eastern did not get on the field on defense in Week 9 and was inactive for Seattle’s Week 10 win in Las Vegas. In a corresponding move, the Seahawks released quarterback and former UFL MVP Adrian Martinez from the practice squad, in the latest sign they expect Sam Darnold to be back in the fold as they emerge from their bye week.

title: Seahawks Reacts Survey: Who should Seattle start at quarterback vs. the 49ers?
summary: Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Seahawks fans and fans across the country. Why yes, we’re starting out the week with more Sam Darnold vs. Drew Lock discourse. If it was only a few years ago that we were […]
full_text: Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Seahawks fans and fans across the country. Why yes, we’re starting out the week with more Sam Darnold vs. Drew Lock discourse. If it was only a few years ago that we were doing the same thing with Geno Smith and Drew Lock, it’s because we literally were and Drew hadn’t even played but a handful of snaps. Geno’s turnover problem wasn’t even at its worst point of the season when we did that discussion post in 2023! But these are bigger stakes and this is much more of a legitimate debate. Drew Lock is 3-0 as a starter and functionally 4-0 when you consider the New England Patriots game a quasi-start. He hasn’t thrown an interception, he’s thrown seven touchdowns, made a lot of difficult throws, and even if the offense isn’t scoring a lot, they don’t look as dysfunctional as we’ve seen with Sam Darnold for much of the year. Lock has looked better than Darnold even ignoring the context of opponents. Drew Lock this season: -EPA per dropback: +0.32 (2nd) -Passer rating: 125.6 (1st) -Yards per attempt: 9 (2nd) -Completion percentage: 73.1% (2nd) pic.twitter.com/O5Om2eXNqP — Ian Hartitz (@Ihartitz) November 16, 2026 But… yeah, the opponents have to matter a little bit, right? This is entering the Raiders game, and while Lock isn’t in this graphic, you’ll notice that Darnold has spent nearly 70% of his dropbacks playing no worse than a “good” defense. Which QBs actually perform against elite defenses, and who's just stat-padding against bad ones? 👀 QB EPA/Play by Defensive Tier | Weeks 1–9 pic.twitter.com/sel9FF99d5 — SFdata9ers🏈📊 (@sfdata9ers) November 13, 2026 As of Week 10, all of Lock’s snaps have come against bad pass defenses. The New England Patriots are 25th, the Las Vegas Raiders are 28th, and the Arizona Cardinals are 32nd in EPA/dropback. It is obviously a very good thing that Lock has outclassed poor defenses, but is that sample size enough to assume that he’ll play like that against competent defenses? Mike Macdonald is going with Sam as his quarterback , and it sounds like he’ll be good to go for what might be a do-or-die game against the 49ers. Given Darnold’s issues with turnovers, decision-making, and frankly some moments where his health is a legitimate question mark, that may not be the most popular decision… and especially not when Drew is making some really impressive plays. BIG PLAY JSN 😮‍💨 @jaxon_smith1 71 YARDS TO THE HOUSE. 📺: @NFLonCBS pic.twitter.com/0sDwRbuiOK — Seattle Seahawks (@Seahawks) November 15, 2026 Right now, Drew is the hot hand. He’s done an exemplary job as a backup QB. But is at least the first half of Sam Darnold’s 2025 and most of 2024 all just a mirage? An aberration? Is this the point of no return for Darnold? Or has the Week 1 injury and subsequent ailments (not to mention the seemingly uneven chemistry with Brian Fleury as his OC) already derailed his season? All of this is to say: If we are on the assumption that Darnold is healthy enough to play Week 12 against the 49ers unencumbered—I’ll be careful with “fully healthy” as a phrase—should the Seahawks still ride the “hot hand” and go with Lock or should they go with Sam? It’s an either/or question but you can add in your own coloring for “Start Sam, but a short leash” or “Bench Sam permanently” or “Start Drew, but play Sam if Drew struggles” type of expansion to your answer in the comments section. Vote below! Oh yeah and there’s a confidence question but you know that already. Who should start at QB? Are you confident in the Seahawks? Sign up here to participate in the weekly emailed surveys: Check back at the end of the week for the full results!

title: Seahawks Week 11 national power rankings: Is Seattle ready for the late season playoff push?
summary: Entering Week 10, the Seattle Seahawks continued to drop down power rankings despite defeating the Arizona Cardinals. Will that downward slide continue after the Seahawks second straight victory over the Las Vegas Raiders? Let’s take a look at five national media sites (NFL.com, CBS Sports, Bleacher Report (B/R), Pro Football Talk (PFT), and ESPN) to […]
full_text: Entering Week 10, the Seattle Seahawks continued to drop down power rankings despite defeating the Arizona Cardinals . Will that downward slide continue after the Seahawks second straight victory over the Las Vegas Raiders? Let’s take a look at five national media sites (NFL.com, CBS Sports, Bleacher Report (B/R), Pro Football Talk (PFT), and ESPN) to see where they rank Seattle. Despite moving down power rankings after a victory last week, that trend will not continue this week … well at least for most national media sites. Let’s start with the one national media site who did continue to move the Seahawks down despite two straight wins. NFL.com moved Seattle down two more spots, from 9th to 11th best in the league. In support of this continued move down is their caution about the offense. Although the offense is slowly starting to improve, “a win over the Raiders is not a great barometer for where it is in this process.” CBS Sports did move the Seahawks up this week, from 14 to 12 , however they still provide the Seahawks the lowest power ranking amongst the five polled national media sites. CBS Sports noted that Drew Lock is 3-0 as starter and raised the question as to whether he should continue starting over Sam Darnold. Speaking of Darnold, B/R raises the question as to whether Darnold will be able to shake his turnover issues when he returns from injury. B/R, who ranked Seattle at number 10 , also note that a 6-4 record for the Seahawks warrant a changing of expectations, those being simply making the playoffs. ESPN, who discussed the NFL team’s non-QB MVP at midseason in this week’s power rankings, placed Seattle as the 9th best team in the league , same as last week. As for who the Seahawks’ non-QB MVP is at this point of the season, they provide the obvious answer: Jaxon Smith-Njigba. ESPN cites an eye opening stat from Elias Sports Bureau for JSN, that being that JSN has the “highest percentage of a team’s receiving yards (52%) through 10 games since 1966.” With numbers like that, perhaps JSN could actually be a legitimate NFL MVP candidate. The highest ranking this week comes from PFT, who rank Seattle as the 8th best team in the league, one spot up from last week. PFT also continued the quarterback controversy talk, stating “Take your time, Sam.” Overall the national landscape remains skeptical over the offense, particularly with Sam Darnold. However, the national media also continue to rave about the team’s defense, JSN, and a notably improving run game. Entering Week 10, the average power rankings between the five polled sites was 10.6. Entering Week 11, that average has slowly risen to an even 10.0. The Seahawks enter a Bye week in Week 11 with eyes set on the San Francisco 49ers in Week 12.
